questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your loop calls the Messages API exactly three times per customer request, executing any requested tools between calls. Logs show some billing disputes are cut off mid-investigation, while simple order-status questions waste calls after Claude has already answered. How should you change the loop's control flow?

options.text: Raise the fixed count to ten iterations so complex disputes have room to finish, and accept the extra calls on simple requests.
Classify each request as simple or complex up front and assign it a fixed iteration budget that matches the predicted difficulty.
Keep looping while stop_reason is "tool_use", and finish when it is "end_turn".
Ask Claude to state how many more steps it expects in each response and stop when the estimate reaches zero.

questions.explanation: The stop_reason field is the model's own signal: "tool_use" means it needs tool results to continue, and "end_turn" means it has finished. Driving the loop from that signal lets short requests end early and long investigations run as long as they need. A larger fixed count (A) still truncates some cases and wastes calls on others. A pre-classifier (B) adds a component whose guesses can be wrong and still imposes arbitrary caps. Self-estimated step counts (D) are unreliable natural-language signals, not a protocol-level completion indicator.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your custom loop ends as soon as a response contains a text block, treating that text as the final answer. Engineers report the agent often stops right after saying things like 'Let me check the config loader next' without ever reading the file. What is the root cause?

options.text: A response can contain explanatory text and a tool_use block together, so text is not a completion signal; the loop should check stop_reason instead.
The system prompt allows the model to narrate its plan, so it should be told to emit tool calls only, with no accompanying text, whenever it intends to act on files.
The Read tool's description is too vague, so the model announces its intent to read files but does not actually choose the tool.
The max_tokens setting is too low, so the response is truncated after the narration and before the tool call is generated.

questions.explanation: Claude regularly returns a text block explaining its next step alongside a tool_use block in the same response, with stop_reason "tool_use". A loop that treats any assistant text as completion therefore exits while a tool call is still pending. Banning narration (B) treats the symptom and removes useful reasoning without fixing the faulty termination check. The tool was in fact requested, so its description (C) is not the issue. Truncation (D) would show stop_reason "max_tokens", not a complete tool request.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The agent keeps calling lookup_order with the same order number three or four times before answering. Your loop executes each tool, writes the result to your logging system, and then sends the next request with the original messages plus a user note saying 'Tool executed.' What should you fix?

options.text: Add a deduplication cache in the MCP server so repeated lookup_order calls with identical arguments return instantly without hitting the backend.
Instruct the model in the system prompt never to call the same tool twice with the same arguments within one conversation.
Lower the temperature so the model is less likely to repeat tool calls it has already made earlier in the conversation.
Append the assistant's tool_use turn and a tool_result block carrying the actual output to the messages before the next request.

questions.explanation: The model can only reason about information that is in the conversation history; if the tool output never reaches it, it rationally asks for the same data again. Appending the assistant turn and a tool_result with the matching tool_use_id gives Claude the order details it needs for its next decision. A cache (A) makes the repeated calls cheaper but leaves the model just as blind. A prompt rule (B) would stop it retrying but it still would not have the data. Temperature (C) has nothing to do with missing context.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A stakeholder wants predictability and proposes replacing the coordinator's model-driven delegation with a hard-coded sequence: always search, then analyze, then synthesize, then report. Queries range from one-line fact checks to multi-week literature surveys. What is the best response?

options.text: Adopt the fixed sequence, since deterministic pipelines are always more reliable than letting a model choose its next action.
Keep model-driven delegation, because the right next step depends on what earlier results reveal, and use code-level enforcement only for rules that must always hold.
Adopt the fixed sequence but let each subagent skip its step when it judges that the step is unnecessary for the query.
Build a decision tree covering every query type the team has seen so far, route anything unrecognized to a human researcher, and update the tree each quarter as new query types appear.

questions.explanation: Open-ended research is the case where model-driven decisions pay off: Claude picks the next action based on the context so far, such as skipping analysis for a fact check or searching again when a gap appears. Deterministic code still belongs where a rule must be guaranteed, but not as a replacement for adaptive orchestration. A fixed pipeline (A) wastes work on simple queries and cannot react to what it finds. Letting subagents skip steps (C) pushes orchestration decisions to agents that lack the overall picture. An exhaustive decision tree (D) breaks on query types nobody anticipated and adds manual load.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. When the agent generates large boilerplate files, users sometimes receive a half-finished answer. Logs show those responses ended with stop_reason "max_tokens" and a final tool_use block that was cut off. Your loop treats every stop_reason other than "tool_use" as completion. What should you change?

options.text: Treat "max_tokens" as completion but append a note telling the user that the output may have been truncated.
Split every generation request into fixed 200-line chunks so that no single response can approach the output limit, and stitch the chunks together in the loop afterward.
Handle "max_tokens" separately: retry with a higher limit, or continue the response, instead of treating it as done.
Parse the partial tool_use JSON, fill in any missing fields with defaults, and execute the reconstructed tool call.

questions.explanation: "max_tokens" means generation hit your output limit, not that the task is finished, so it needs its own branch in the loop. When the truncated response ends in an incomplete tool_use block, retrying with a higher limit lets the full tool call come through. Labeling truncated output as complete (A) still ships a broken result. Fixed chunking (B) is an arbitrary workaround that complicates every request. Guessing at missing fields (D) runs tool calls the model never actually made.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are adding a max-turns limit to an Agent SDK agent that automates repetitive refactors. Which TWO statements describe the right role for that limit? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: It is a safety net against runaway loops, while normal termination still comes from the model finishing with no further tool calls.
It should be the main way the agent decides it has finished, so set it to the typical number of steps a refactor needs on average.
Hitting the limit should be handled as an incomplete run, reported as partial and resumable, rather than as success.
Setting it to one turn is a good way to make the agent produce more concise refactors with fewer edits overall.
Once a turn limit exists, the loop no longer needs to look at why the model stopped on each response.

questions.explanation: Turn and budget limits are guardrails for open-ended or misbehaving runs; the agent should normally end because Claude produces a response with no tool calls. When the cap is hit, the SDK reports an error_max_turns result, which you should treat as unfinished work you can resume with a higher limit. Using the cap as the primary stop mechanism (B) is the arbitrary-iteration-cap anti-pattern. A one-turn cap (D) simply prevents multi-step work. A cap does not replace stop handling (E), because most runs should end well before it.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Claude returns one response containing two tool_use blocks, get_customer and lookup_order. Your loop executes only the first block and sends back a single tool_result, and the next API call fails with an error about tool_use ids without matching results. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Set the system prompt to instruct Claude to request only one tool per response so the loop never receives more than one.
Execute every tool_use block in the response and return one tool_result per block, each matched by tool_use_id, in the next user message.
Execute the first block, drop the second block from the stored assistant turn so the history stays consistent, and let Claude ask for it again later if it still needs it.
Retry the same request until Claude returns a response that contains exactly one tool_use block, then continue normally.

questions.explanation: Claude may request several tools in a single turn, and the API expects a tool_result for every tool_use id immediately after that turn. Running all requested tools and returning all results keeps the conversation valid and lets independent lookups happen together. Forbidding parallel calls (A) slows the agent to avoid a bug in your loop. Editing the stored assistant turn (C) corrupts the history the model reasons over. Retrying until you get one call (D) wastes requests and still never fixes the loop.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. When the document-fetch tool hits a paywalled URL, your tool handler raises an exception that escapes the loop and aborts the whole research run. Other sources for the same claim are usually available. How should the loop handle tool failures?

options.text: Remove the document-fetch tool for the rest of the run after its first failure so the model cannot hit the same error twice.
Catch the failure and return an empty successful result so the run can continue without interrupting the model's reasoning.
Retry the same URL with exponential backoff until it succeeds, and only then return the document to the model, so it never has to reason about failed or partial fetches at all.
Catch the failure and return it to Claude as an error tool_result describing what went wrong, so it can choose another source or approach.

questions.explanation: Tool failures are information the model can act on, so they belong in the conversation as a tool_result flagged as an error with a useful description. Claude can then try a different source, adjust the query, or note the gap. Returning an empty success (B) hides the failure and invites the model to conclude the source had nothing. A paywall is not transient, so backoff (C) retries a call that will never succeed. Removing the tool (A) throws away a capability that works for most URLs.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. To save time, a developer let the synthesis subagent call the web search subagent directly through a shared message queue. Since then, failed searches go unnoticed, retries are inconsistent, and nobody can reconstruct why a claim appeared in a report. What is the best architectural fix?

options.text: Add detailed logging and tracing to the shared queue so every message exchanged between subagents is recorded, searchable, and available for later debugging of failed runs.
Give the synthesis subagent its own retry policy that mirrors the coordinator's, so errors are handled the same way.
Merge the search and synthesis subagents into a single agent so that no inter-agent messaging is needed at all.
Route all communication between subagents through the coordinator, which handles delegation, errors, and information flow.

questions.explanation: In a hub-and-spoke design the coordinator is the single place where delegation, error handling, and information routing happen, which gives consistent recovery and a traceable record of how each result was produced. The direct side channel bypasses all of that. Logging the queue (A) improves the record but leaves error handling scattered. Copying retry logic into each subagent (B) duplicates policy and will drift. Merging the agents (C) gives up the specialization and context isolation that motivated the design.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Usage analytics show 40% of queries are simple lookups, such as the founding year of a company, yet every query runs search, document analysis, synthesis, and report generation. Costs and latency are high for these queries. What should you change?

options.text: Add a cache of previous answers so that repeated simple lookups skip the pipeline entirely on a cache hit.
Have the coordinator assess each query's requirements and invoke only the subagents it actually needs.
Run all four subagents in parallel instead of sequentially so the full pipeline finishes in less time.
Switch every subagent to a smaller model so the full pipeline costs less for every type of query.

questions.explanation: Part of the coordinator's job is to scale effort to the query: a fact lookup might need a single search, while a survey needs several specialists. Selecting subagents dynamically removes the waste at its source. A cache (A) only helps repeated questions and leaves novel simple queries just as expensive. Parallelizing (C) cuts latency but keeps all the unnecessary work, and the stages depend on each other anyway. Downgrading every model (D) reduces cost per call but can hurt quality on the complex queries that need it.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. For the topic 'battery recycling economics', the coordinator spawns three search subagents with the instruction 'research battery recycling economics'. Their results overlap by about 70%, citing the same handful of articles. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Deduplicate the three result sets in the synthesis subagent before it starts writing the combined findings.
Reduce the search stage to one subagent, since three agents with the same task will always find the same sources.
Give each subagent a distinct slice of the scope, such as a separate subtopic or source type, in its assignment.
Raise each subagent's temperature so that their search queries diverge more from one another on each run.

questions.explanation: Subagents given identical, vague instructions naturally repeat each other's work. Partitioning the scope, for example by subtopic (collection costs, processing, policy) or by source type (academic, industry, regulatory), gives each one distinct ground to cover and widens overall coverage. Deduplicating afterward (A) removes redundancy but recovers none of the missed coverage. A single subagent (B) loses the breadth and parallelism. Higher temperature (D) adds randomness, not a deliberate division of labor.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The synthesis subagent's drafts often include notes like 'no sources found on EU regulatory treatment'. The coordinator currently passes each draft straight to the report subagent. How should you improve coverage?

options.text: Have the report subagent remove any section that has gaps so the final report only contains fully supported material.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to fill gaps from its own general knowledge whenever the search results do not cover a section.
Increase the number of search results each subagent returns on the first pass, from 10 to 50, so that gaps are much less likely to occur and follow-up passes become unnecessary.
Have the coordinator review each draft for gaps, send targeted queries back to the search and analysis subagents, and re-run synthesis until coverage is sufficient.

questions.explanation: An iterative refinement loop uses the synthesis output as a diagnostic: the coordinator spots gaps, re-delegates with targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage meets the bar. That closes gaps with sourced evidence. Filling gaps from model knowledge (B) brings in uncited and possibly outdated claims. More results on the first pass (C) is a blunt instrument that may still miss the specific topic. Deleting gapped sections (A) hides incompleteness instead of fixing it.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Early in the session the user told the coordinator to use only peer-reviewed sources published after 2022. The document analysis subagent still cites 2019 blog posts. The coordinator's delegation message reads 'Analyze the documents on solid-state batteries.' What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The analysis subagent's model ignores constraints it receives and needs a stronger model that follows instructions more closely.
The subagent's context is isolated, so it never saw the user's constraint; the coordinator must state it in the delegation.
The search subagent returned old blog posts, and the analysis subagent cannot reject documents that it is given.
The constraint was overwritten when the coordinator's context was compacted, and should be stored in a project memory file.

questions.explanation: Subagents start with their own fresh context and do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history, so a constraint the user gave the coordinator is invisible to them unless it is written into the delegation. Including the source requirements in the subagent's prompt fixes the problem directly. A stronger model (A) cannot follow an instruction it never received. Blaming the search subagent (C) ignores that the analysis subagent was never told what to reject. Compaction (D) is speculative, and the delegation message shows the constraint was simply left out.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. You are writing the coordinator's system prompt. Which TWO responsibilities should belong to the coordinator rather than to the individual subagents? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Breaking the research question into subtasks and choosing which subagents to invoke for them.
Letting the search subagent forward its results straight to the report generator to save a round trip.
Collecting subagent results, handling their failures, and deciding what goes to synthesis next.
Giving every subagent the full tool set so any one of them can cover for another that fails.
Having subagents retry one another's failed tasks peer to peer without involving anyone else.

questions.explanation: The coordinator owns task decomposition and delegation, and it aggregates results, handles errors, and routes information. Keeping these in one place gives consistent behavior and observability. Direct forwarding between subagents (B) and peer-to-peer retries (E) bypass the hub and scatter control. Giving every subagent every tool (D) blurs specializations and makes tool selection less reliable.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Reviewing past runs, you find the coordinator often splits broad topics into a few closely related subtasks. For example, 'cybersecurity risks for hospitals' became three ransomware subtasks, with nothing on medical device or insider threats. Which change to the coordinator's prompt best prevents this?

options.text: Require the coordinator to always create at least eight subtasks so that broad topics receive more total research effort.
Tell the synthesis subagent to add a section on any major dimension it believes is missing from the findings.
Let each search subagent broaden its own query whenever it suspects its assignment is too narrow for the topic.
Have the coordinator list the topic's major dimensions first and check that its subtasks cover them before delegating.

questions.explanation: The gap is created at decomposition time, so the fix belongs in the coordinator: mapping the breadth of the topic and checking subtasks against it before delegating stops overly narrow plans. A minimum subtask count (A) can produce eight ransomware subtasks just as easily. Asking synthesis to add missing sections (B) invites unsourced content after research is over. Letting subagents broaden their own scope (C) produces overlap and drift, because no single subagent sees the overall plan.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A teammate proposes splitting your single agent that generates CRUD boilerplate from a schema file into five cooperating agents: planner, model writer, controller writer, test writer, and reviewer. The current agent finishes in under a minute with high acceptance rates. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Adopt the five-agent design, since specialized agents always outperform a generalist agent on code generation tasks.
Adopt the design but run the five agents in parallel so the extra coordination does not add any latency.
Keep the single agent, and reach for subagents only when work is parallelizable or would overload one context.
Keep the single agent but add a reviewer subagent to every run, since independent review is always worth the cost.

questions.explanation: Multi-agent designs add coordination overhead, token cost, and new failure points, so they pay off when subtasks are independent and parallelizable or when exploration would flood a single context. A fast, well-scoped generator with good acceptance rates has neither problem, so the simplest working design should stay. Specialization does not automatically win (A). The steps depend on each other, so parallelizing them (B) does not fit. Adding a reviewer to every run (D) adds cost when there is no quality problem to solve.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. In local interactive testing the coordinator delegates to its subagents correctly. Deployed as a headless Agent SDK service with no approval callback, logs show its subagent-spawning tool calls (the Agent tool, called Task in older versions) are rejected, and the coordinator does all the research itself. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether each subagent's description is detailed enough for the coordinator to recognize when to delegate, since vague descriptions are a common reason delegation fails in production.
Whether the subagents' own tool lists include the search and fetch tools that they need to do their work.
Whether the coordinator's model is capable enough to orchestrate several subagents at once in production.
Whether the coordinator's allowed tools include the subagent-spawning tool, since headless calls needing approval are denied.

questions.explanation: Delegation happens through the subagent-spawning tool, so the coordinator needs permission to use it. In a headless deployment with no approval callback, tool calls that are not pre-approved and need approval are denied, which matches the logs. The coordinator is choosing to delegate, so descriptions (A) and model capability (C) are not the problem. Subagent tool lists (B) only matter once a subagent actually starts, and here none does.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The synthesis subagent's output is fluent but generic and rarely cites the specific statistics the search and analysis subagents found. The coordinator invokes synthesis with the prompt 'Synthesize the findings from the search and analysis agents into a cohesive summary.' What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Include the complete outputs of the search and analysis subagents directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt.
Give the synthesis subagent access to the web search tools so it can find the statistics again on its own.
Add few-shot examples of high-quality syntheses to the synthesis subagent's system prompt to raise its standard.
Tell the synthesis subagent to read the other subagents' transcripts from the shared session before it begins writing.

questions.explanation: The synthesis subagent has no access to earlier findings unless they are passed in its prompt; with only a one-line instruction, it can only write generically. Putting the full search results and analysis outputs into the delegation gives it the material to synthesize. Re-searching (B) duplicates work and blurs the agents' roles. Few-shot examples (C) improve style but cannot provide missing facts. Subagents do not get the parent's conversation or other subagents' tool results in their context (D), so the instruction would not help.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Final reports increasingly attribute statistics to the wrong source, or cite sources by name with no page reference. The analysis subagent currently returns findings as flowing paragraphs, with source names worked into the prose. What change best preserves attribution through synthesis?

options.text: Instruct the synthesis subagent to double-check each citation against the original documents before it writes the report, re-fetching any document whose citation looks inconsistent.
Ask the analysis subagent to write longer paragraphs that repeat the full source name next to every claim it makes.
Have the report subagent append a bibliography of every source consulted during the run at the end of each report.
Have the analysis subagent return structured records that keep each claim separate from its source URL, document, page, and date.

questions.explanation: Separating content from metadata in a structured format makes the mapping from claim to source explicit and machine-preservable, so downstream agents can carry it through merging and rewriting. Prose with embedded names is easy to garble when it is summarized. Re-verifying every citation (A) is expensive and treats the symptom. Repeating source names in longer prose (B) is still unstructured and adds tokens. A bibliography (C) lists sources but does not say which claim came from which page.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. For a comparison across four markets, the coordinator spawns one search subagent per market, but it does so across four consecutive turns and waits for each to finish before spawning the next. The searches are independent of one another. How do you cut latency?

options.text: Merge the four market assignments into a single search subagent that researches all four markets in one context.
Have the coordinator emit all four subagent-spawning tool calls in a single response so they run concurrently.
Switch the search subagents to a faster, smaller model so that each one of the sequential runs completes sooner.
Cap each search subagent's turns so that every sequential run finishes within a fixed amount of time.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent tasks can run in parallel when the coordinator issues the spawning calls together in one response, so total time approaches that of the slowest task instead of the sum of all four. A single combined subagent (A) is sequential by nature and crowds one context. A smaller model (C) or turn caps (D) shave time off each run while keeping the unnecessary serialization, and may reduce research quality.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The coordinator's delegation prompts give search subagents a rigid 12-step procedure, such as 'Step 3: query Google Scholar with the exact title phrase'. When a step's source has nothing relevant, subagents either stall or return thin results. How should you rewrite the delegation prompts?

options.text: State the research goal, the expected output format, and the quality bar, and let each subagent choose how to meet them.
Add fallback branches to each of the 12 steps that specify exactly which alternative source to query and how many times to retry when that step's source has no relevant results.
Shorten the procedure to the five most productive steps so that subagents waste less effort on dead ends.
Replace the procedure with a single instruction to search thoroughly and return whatever looks relevant to the topic.

questions.explanation: Delegating goals and quality criteria rather than procedures lets subagents adapt when a planned source comes up empty while still producing what the coordinator needs. Clear objectives, output formats, and boundaries are what make delegation effective. Adding branches (B) makes the script longer and more brittle against cases nobody anticipated. A shorter script (C) is still a script. A vague instruction (D) drops the objective and quality bar that subagents need to stay on task.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You defined a code-reviewer subagent with AgentDefinition, a clear description, and a system prompt telling it never to modify files. Twice it has 'fixed' issues it found by editing source files. How should you prevent this?

options.text: Strengthen the subagent's system prompt with capitalized warnings and an example of a review that makes no edits.
Have the coordinator ask the reviewer to confirm in its final report that it did not modify any files.
Set the subagent's tools list to read-only tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob so it cannot edit files at all.
Run git checkout after every review to discard any changes the reviewer may have made to the working tree.

questions.explanation: An AgentDefinition's tools field controls which tools a subagent has, and a tool left out is not in its session at all. Restricting the reviewer to read-only tools makes edits impossible rather than discouraged. Stronger prompt wording (A) is still probabilistic, which is how the problem arose. Self-reported confirmation (B) does not prevent anything. Reverting afterward (D) is a fragile cleanup that can also throw away legitimate changes others made in the same tree.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You defined two subagents: 'analyzer', described as 'Analyzes code', and 'inspector', described as 'Inspects the codebase'. One maps dependencies and the other finds security issues, but the main agent picks the wrong one about half the time. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Merge the two subagents into one that does both dependency mapping and security review in every run.
Write descriptions that say what each subagent does and when to use it, such as 'Use for tracing module dependencies'.
Add a keyword-based router in front of the main agent that inspects each request and picks the subagent before Claude sees it, using terms like 'dependency' or 'vulnerability'.
Give the two subagents different models so the main agent can tell them apart by their capability levels.

questions.explanation: Claude chooses which subagent to invoke from each AgentDefinition's description, so two vague, near-identical descriptions produce coin-flip routing. Clear, distinct descriptions that say when to use each one fix the root cause at almost no cost. Merging them (A) throws away the specialization. A keyword router (C) is over-engineered and bypasses the model's understanding of the request. The model setting (D) has no bearing on which subagent gets chosen.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. On Monday a 'legacy-mapper' subagent mapped the billing module. On Tuesday the main agent invokes legacy-mapper again in a new run to map the adjacent invoicing module, and it re-discovers everything about billing from scratch. Which TWO approaches correctly give it Monday's knowledge? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Pass the key findings from Monday's run directly in the prompt of Tuesday's new invocation.
Rely on the subagent's name, since invocations of the same named subagent share memory automatically.
Resume Monday's session and resume that subagent by its agent ID so it keeps its earlier transcript.
Set the subagent's model to 'inherit' so that it shares the main agent's memory of the previous day.
Put the findings only in the main agent's system prompt, which every subagent reads when it starts up.

questions.explanation: Subagents do not share memory between invocations, so earlier findings must either be passed explicitly in the new prompt or recovered by resuming the original session and that specific subagent, which keeps its full prior history. A shared name (B) gives no shared state. 'inherit' (D) only selects the same model, not shared memory. Non-fork subagents do not receive the parent's system prompt (E).

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Policy says the agent may change an account's email address only after the customer passes one-time-code verification through verify_identity. The system prompt states this clearly, but an audit finds about 2% of email changes happened without a successful verification. What should you implement?

options.text: Move the verification rule to the top of the system prompt and add three examples of the correct verification order.
Have the agent restate its verification status before every account change so that skipped steps become visible.
Review a weekly sample of email changes and retrain support staff on reversing changes that were unverified.
Block update_email in code until verify_identity has returned success for this customer in the current session.

questions.explanation: When a step is a hard prerequisite for a sensitive action, a programmatic gate that blocks the downstream tool until the prerequisite succeeds gives a deterministic guarantee. Prompt instructions keep a non-zero failure rate, which is exactly what the audit found. Rewording or examples (A) may reduce the rate but cannot eliminate it. Self-reported status (B) is still model-generated text that can be wrong. Sampling and cleanup (C) detects violations after the account has already been exposed.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Human agents who take escalations cannot see the AI conversation transcript. They complain that escalate_to_human tickets say only things like 'Customer needs help with a refund', so they must re-ask everything and customers get frustrated. What should the escalation include?

options.text: A short apology for the customer and a note telling the human agent to call the customer back for the details.
The full raw conversation transcript pasted into the ticket body, including every tool call and result, so the human agent has every detail of the conversation available to read.
A sentiment score and a priority level so that human agents can triage the most frustrated customers first in the queue.
A structured summary with the customer ID, the issue, the root cause found, actions already taken, any amounts involved, and a recommended next step.

questions.explanation: A structured handoff gives the receiving human exactly what they need to act without the transcript: who the customer is, what was found, what was already done, and what to do next. Pasting the raw transcript (B) dumps the work of extracting those facts onto the human, assuming the ticketing system can even hold it. Sentiment and priority (C) help triage but say nothing about the case itself. Telling the human to call back (A) is exactly the re-asking the team wants to avoid.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer writes: 'I was charged twice for order 4411, the blender in order 4502 arrived cracked, and I need to change the shipping address on order 4630.' The agent resolves the double charge and ends the conversation, and the customer has to contact support twice more. What design change best addresses this?

options.text: Ask the customer to submit each issue as a separate request so that the agent can handle one concern per conversation.
Have the agent split the message into distinct issues, investigate each one using the shared customer context, and send one combined resolution.
Route any message that mentions more than one order number straight to a human agent, since multi-issue cases are complex and more likely to need policy judgment than single-issue ones.
Increase max_tokens so that the agent has room to write a longer response covering all of the customer's issues.

questions.explanation: Multi-concern requests should be broken into separate items, each investigated with the shared customer context (independent lookups can run in parallel), and then combined into one coherent reply. That directly targets first-contact resolution. Making the customer split the request (A) pushes the agent's job onto them. Escalating every multi-issue case (C) gives up resolutions the agent is capable of. Output length (D) was never the constraint; the agent never investigated the other two issues.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. After you added 'You MUST call get_customer before process_refund' to the system prompt, a 200-conversation test suite passed with no violations. A product manager asks why you still plan to add a code-level prerequisite check. Which justification is strongest?

options.text: Test suites never reflect production traffic, so their results should be ignored when you design any agent safeguard, and every prompt rule should be duplicated in code as a matter of course.
Code-level checks make the agent respond faster, because the model has fewer instructions in its system prompt to read.
Prompt compliance is probabilistic, and at production volume even a small miss rate on refunds causes real financial errors that a code check prevents.
The model forgets system prompt instructions after a few turns, so any rule placed there stops applying in long conversations.

questions.explanation: Zero failures in 200 tests is consistent with a small but real failure rate, which becomes many wrong refunds across thousands of daily conversations. When the cost of a miss is financial, a deterministic gate is justified even when the prompt usually works. Ignoring tests entirely (A) overstates the point. Speed (B) is not the reason for the gate. The claim that models forget system prompts after a few turns (D) is not an accurate description of how system prompts work.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your prerequisite gate lets process_refund run once get_customer has been called at least once in the session. In one incident the caller verified as customer A, mentioned a spouse's order, and the agent refunded an order that belongs to customer B. How should you tighten the gate?

options.text: Have the gate also check that the order being refunded belongs to the customer ID that get_customer verified.
Tell the agent in the system prompt never to process refunds on orders that belong to a different customer.
Require get_customer to be called again immediately before every process_refund call, whatever ID it returns.
Remove lookup_order access for orders that are outside the current session until a human approves the lookup.

questions.explanation: A gate that only checks whether a prerequisite step happened can be satisfied by the wrong data. Binding the verified customer ID to the downstream call's arguments makes the guarantee mean what the business needs: refunds only on the verified customer's own orders. A prompt rule (B) reintroduces probabilistic compliance. Calling get_customer again (C) proves nothing if the refund still targets someone else's order. Blocking lookups (D) is heavier than needed and does not stop the wrong refund once an order has been fetched.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your new gate blocks process_refund when no verified customer ID exists, but it returns only 'Error'. Logs show the agent then retries process_refund repeatedly or tells the customer that the refund system is down. What should the blocked call return?

options.text: Nothing at all, so the agent does not see the failure and simply moves on to the next part of the request.
A fake success message, so the conversation continues while a background job queues the refund for later review.
A clear explanation that identity verification is required first and that get_customer is the step to complete.
A generic 'temporarily unavailable' message, so the agent waits and tries again a little later in the session.

questions.explanation: When enforcement blocks an action, the model should learn why and what would unblock it, so it can recover by verifying the customer and then retrying. A bare 'Error' or a false 'unavailable' message (D) leads to pointless retries and misleading statements to customers. Hiding the block (A) leaves the agent unaware the refund never happened. A fake success (B) causes the agent to tell the customer something untrue.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are reviewing which workflow rules need code-level enforcement and which can stay as prompt guidance. Which TWO rules most warrant programmatic enforcement? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The customer's identity must be verified before any refund or account change is processed.
Responses should open by acknowledging the customer's issue in a warm and friendly tone.
Refunds above the policy limit must not be processed without approval from a human.
The agent should summarize the customer's order history in a few concise bullet points.
The agent should apologize whenever a shipment has been delayed by more than a week from the original estimate.

questions.explanation: Rules whose violation causes financial loss or security exposure, such as identity verification and refund limits, need deterministic enforcement because prompt compliance always has some failure rate. Tone, summarization style, and apology conventions (B, D, E) are quality preferences where an occasional miss is tolerable. Prompt guidance and examples handle those well, and code checks would add complexity with little benefit.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. After a successful launch of refund gating, an engineer proposes adding code-level hooks for every conversational step: greet first, restate the issue, offer help articles, and close with a satisfaction question. Each would block the agent's reply until the step is detected. What is the best response?

options.text: Approve all of the hooks, because deterministic enforcement is always preferable to relying on the model's judgment.
Keep code enforcement for high-consequence rules, and handle conversational style through the prompt and examples.
Approve the hooks but have them log violations instead of blocking, so that the team can review them weekly.
Replace the agent's conversational flow with fixed scripted templates so that every step happens in order every time.

questions.explanation: Programmatic enforcement is worth its rigidity and maintenance cost when a violation has material consequences. Conversational steps vary legitimately; a customer who asks a direct question may not need a greeting and restatement first, so blocking replies on them would hurt the experience. Prompt guidance with examples fits those preferences. Enforcing everything in code (A) makes the agent brittle. Logging-only hooks (C) add infrastructure for what are style questions. Scripted templates (D) give up the flexibility that drives resolution on ambiguous requests.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. lookup_order returns order dates as Unix epoch seconds, the shipping MCP tool returns ISO 8601 strings, and the returns MCP tool returns 'MM/DD/YY'. The agent sometimes misjudges whether an item is within the 30-day return window. You cannot change the MCP servers. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add a section to the system prompt explaining each tool's date format, with worked conversion examples, and instruct the agent to convert every date to ISO 8601 before reasoning about return windows.
Add few-shot examples that show the agent correctly computing return windows from mixed date formats.
Ask the agent to explain its date calculation step by step before it decides whether a return is eligible.
Add a PostToolUse hook that converts every date in these tool results to ISO 8601 before the model sees them.

questions.explanation: A PostToolUse hook can transform tool results before Claude processes them, so normalizing all dates into one format in code removes the ambiguity entirely. This works without touching the third-party servers. Prompt explanations (A) and few-shot examples (B) still leave the model doing error-prone conversions on every call. Step-by-step reasoning (C) may help somewhat but keeps the calculation probabilistic when a deterministic transform is easy.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Finance requires that no refund above $500 is ever issued without human approval. The system prompt states this rule, but last month three refunds of $620 to $900 went through. Which approach gives the guarantee finance is asking for?

options.text: Restate the $500 rule in process_refund's tool description so the model sees it at the moment it chooses the tool.
Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that denies any call over $500 and tells the agent to escalate instead.
Run a nightly job that flags refunds over $500 so finance can claw them back from customers the next morning.
Have the agent self-assess its confidence before each refund and escalate whenever confidence is below a threshold.

questions.explanation: A PreToolUse hook intercepts the tool call before it executes, so code can deterministically deny over-limit refunds and redirect the agent to escalation. That is a guarantee rather than a hope. A tool description (A) is still guidance the model can miss. A nightly audit (C) detects violations after the money has left. Self-assessed confidence (D) is poorly calibrated and unrelated to a fixed dollar threshold.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A legacy billing MCP tool you cannot modify returns full card numbers and billing addresses alongside the fields the agent needs. Security requires that card numbers never enter the model's context or the conversation transcript. What should you do?

options.text: Use a PostToolUse hook that replaces the tool's output with a redacted version before Claude sees it.
Tell the agent in the system prompt never to repeat card numbers in any of its responses to customers.
Have a PreToolUse hook deny every call to the billing tool so that its data can never reach the model.
Run a scheduled job that scrubs card numbers out of stored conversation transcripts at the end of each day.

questions.explanation: PostToolUse hooks run after a tool returns and can replace its output before the model processes it, so redacting there keeps the sensitive data out of context and out of the transcript while preserving the fields the agent needs. A prompt rule (B) only limits what the agent says; the numbers would still be in context. Denying the tool (C) removes billing data the agent needs to resolve disputes. Scrubbing afterward (D) leaves the data exposed during the conversation itself.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. To enforce the $500 refund limit, a developer added a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that flags any refund over $500 and sends finance an alert. Refunds over the limit are still being paid out. What is wrong with this design?

options.text: The hook's matcher needs the fully qualified MCP tool name, so it is probably not firing on refund calls at all.
The alert should go to the agent through additional context rather than to finance, so the agent can apologize.
Hooks cannot enforce numeric thresholds reliably, so the limit should be written into the system prompt instead.
PostToolUse runs after the refund has already executed, so the limit must be enforced in a PreToolUse hook.

questions.explanation: PostToolUse fires after a tool has run and returned, which suits transforming or auditing results but cannot stop an action that has already happened. Blocking requires intercepting the outgoing call in PreToolUse. Alerts are reaching finance, which shows the hook is firing, so the matcher (A) is not the problem. Telling the agent after the fact (B) still lets the refund through. Hooks are ordinary code and enforce numeric checks deterministically (C); the problem is only when this one runs.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You registered a PreToolUse hook with matcher 'Write|Edit' that denies any change to files named .env. During a session the agent still overwrote .env, using a Bash command that redirected output into the file. What is the most accurate explanation and fix?

options.text: Hooks only apply to MCP tools, so the protection must move into the system prompt to cover the built-in tools.
The matcher only fires for the tools it names, so Bash also needs coverage, through a Bash hook or sandbox rules.
The deny decision was overridden by the session's permission mode, so the mode must be set to 'plan' instead.
Hooks run asynchronously by default, so the Bash command completed and wrote the file before the hook's deny decision was returned to the agent loop.

questions.explanation: Matchers filter hooks by tool name, so a 'Write|Edit' hook never runs when the agent writes the file through Bash. Protecting the file means also covering the Bash path, for example with a Bash PreToolUse hook that inspects commands or with sandbox filesystem rules. Hooks apply to built-in tools as well as MCP tools (A). The hook never fired, so the permission mode did not override anything (C), and switching to plan mode would block legitimate work. Hooks block by default unless they explicitly return async output (D).

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are writing the PreToolUse hook that handles process_refund calls above the $500 limit. Which behavior should the hook implement when it intercepts such a call?

options.text: Rewrite the amount to $500 with updatedInput and allow the call, so the customer still gets most of the refund.
Throw an exception that terminates the session, so that no further actions can be taken on the customer's account.
Deny the call with a reason saying it exceeds the limit and must go to escalate_to_human with a handoff summary.
Allow the call but mark the refund as pending in the backend, and tell the model that it completed successfully.

questions.explanation: Denying with a clear permissionDecisionReason blocks the violation and tells the model why, so it can follow the alternative workflow and escalate with a structured handoff. Silently changing the amount (A) issues a refund the customer never agreed to and that nobody approved. Killing the session (B) abandons the customer mid-conversation. Telling the model a pending refund succeeded (D) leads it to give the customer false information.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your team is deciding which behaviors to implement as Agent SDK hooks and which to leave to prompt instructions. Which TWO are the best fit for hooks? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Recording an audit entry for every tool call the agent makes, with no gaps.
Encouraging the agent to explain its reasoning in a friendlier, clearer tone.
Blocking any git push to protected branches, whatever reason the agent gives.
Deciding which file is most relevant to read first when exploring a codebase.
Improving the quality and structure of the code summaries the agent writes.

questions.explanation: Hooks are code that runs on every matching event, which makes them right for guarantees: complete audit logging and hard blocks on prohibited actions. Tone, exploration strategy, and summary quality (B, D, E) depend on the model's judgment and are best shaped through prompts and examples. Hooks cannot make those judgment calls well, and trying would put brittle heuristics in place of model reasoning.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. The platform team registered a PreToolUse hook that auto-approves Bash commands starting with 'npm'. Security separately registered a PreToolUse hook that denies any command containing 'npm publish'. A developer worries the two hooks will conflict unpredictably. What actually happens when the agent runs 'npm publish'?

options.text: Whichever hook finishes running first decides the outcome, so the result may vary from one run to the next.
The hook registered first takes precedence, so the auto-approve hook wins if it appears earlier in the config.
The two decisions cancel each other out, so the call falls back to the session's default permission mode.
The deny wins, because the most restrictive decision applies when matching hooks disagree on a tool call.

questions.explanation: Matching hooks run in parallel, and when their permission decisions differ the most restrictive one applies, with deny taking priority over allow. This lets separate teams add independent safety hooks without coordinating order. Completion order (A) affects timing but not which decision wins. Registration order (B) does not set precedence. Conflicting decisions do not cancel out (C); the deny is applied.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer asks the agent to 'add comprehensive tests to our 200k-line legacy billing service', which has almost no existing tests and many undocumented dependencies. How should the agent decompose this task?

options.text: Generate tests file by file in alphabetical order so that every file eventually gets coverage in a predictable way.
Map the structure first, find high-impact areas, then follow a prioritized plan that is revised as dependencies turn up.
Ask the engineer for a complete list of every function that needs tests, ranked by priority, before doing any exploration of the codebase, so the plan reflects the team's knowledge.
Write one end-to-end test that exercises the whole service, since unit tests are not worth the effort in legacy code.

questions.explanation: Open-ended tasks benefit from adaptive decomposition: map the system, identify where tests add the most value (critical paths, frequently changed code), and create a plan that changes as hidden dependencies emerge. Alphabetical coverage (A) spends effort without regard to impact and ignores dependencies. Requiring a complete function list (C) pushes the discovery work onto the engineer. A single end-to-end test (D) does not deliver the comprehensive coverage that was asked for.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Every pull request to an internal service gets the same three checks: API contract compatibility, database migration safety, and logging conventions. The checks rarely change and do not depend on one another's findings. Which decomposition pattern fits best?

options.text: A fixed sequence of focused prompts, one per check, followed by a step that combines their results.
A fully dynamic investigation where the agent decides at runtime which checks each PR might need.
One large prompt that asks for all three checks at once, so the model sees every concern together.
A coordinator with research subagents that each search the web for current best practices per check.

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining suits predictable, multi-aspect reviews: each step gets a focused prompt, which improves depth and consistency, and a final step combines the results. Dynamic decomposition (B) adds unpredictability where the steps are already known. A single combined prompt (C) spreads attention across concerns and tends to make some checks shallow. Web research subagents (D) solve a different problem; the team's standards are already defined.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You switched large PR reviews to per-file analysis passes, and local findings improved. However, a PR shipped where one file renamed a field in an event payload and the consumer in another file still read the old name. Neither per-file pass flagged it. What should you add?

options.text: Return to a single pass over all files so that cross-file relationships are visible to the model in one context.
A separate integration pass that reads the per-file results and the changed interfaces to check data flow across files.
Give each per-file pass the full contents of every other file in the PR so it can check its own dependencies and catch cross-file contract mismatches while it analyzes its file.
Run each per-file pass twice and flag issues found by either run so that fewer real problems are missed.

questions.explanation: Per-file passes give focused local analysis but, by design, cannot see cross-file contracts. Adding a dedicated integration pass that looks at interfaces and data flow between files covers that gap while keeping the local passes focused. Going back to one pass (A) brings back the attention dilution you fixed. Stuffing every file into each pass (C) recreates the same overload many times over. Repeating per-file passes (D) still never looks across files.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Production shows intermittent 502 errors from a service nobody on the current team wrote. The cause could be the load balancer config, connection pool exhaustion, a slow dependency, or something else. How should the agent structure the investigation?

options.text: Run a fixed checklist of the ten most common causes of 502 errors in order and report the first one that matches.
Investigate all four hypotheses fully in parallel before looking at any logs, so that no possible cause is skipped and the team gets a complete picture of every potential failure mode.
Ask the on-call engineer to identify the most likely cause first, and then have the agent confirm that guess only.
Start from the evidence and let each finding decide the next subtask, such as tracing pool metrics after spotting a timeout.

questions.explanation: Open-ended diagnosis is where dynamic decomposition shines: each discovery narrows the space and determines the next useful step, so effort follows the evidence. A fixed checklist (A) can stop at a superficial match and miss causes outside the list. Fully investigating every hypothesis up front (B) wastes effort that early evidence could rule out. Anchoring on one guess (C) risks confirmation bias and does not use the agent's ability to explore.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Your report pipeline is a chain: outline, then draft sections, then format. Occasionally the outline omits a section the client requires, such as methodology, and the whole report must be regenerated after delivery. What is the most efficient fix?

options.text: Add a check between the outline and drafting steps that verifies required sections and sends failures back for revision.
Merge outlining and drafting into one step so the model can notice and add missing required sections while it writes the draft, rather than relying on an outline produced beforehand.
Have the formatting step insert placeholder headings for any required sections that are missing from the draft.
Regenerate every report twice and deliver whichever version contains more of the sections the client requires.

questions.explanation: Prompt chains can include gates between steps that check intermediate output and catch errors before they spread downstream. Validating the outline against the required sections is cheap and stops the expensive rework. Merging the steps (B) loses the focus that chaining provides and does not guarantee the sections appear. Placeholder headings (C) produce reports that look complete but are empty. Double generation (D) doubles cost and still offers no guarantee.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Which TWO of these tasks are best suited to a fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) rather than dynamic, adaptive decomposition? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Generating reference docs for each REST endpoint from its handler, using the same template every time.
Finding the root cause of a memory leak that appears only under certain production traffic patterns.
Converting config files through set steps: validate the old schema, transform it, verify the new schema.
Answering 'how does authentication work here?' in a codebase the team has never looked at before.
Triaging a new kind of incident that has symptoms no runbook or past postmortem has ever described in any detail.

questions.explanation: Fixed pipelines fit when the steps are known in advance and the same for every input, like templated doc generation or a defined validate-transform-verify migration. Memory leak diagnosis, exploring unfamiliar code, and triaging novel incidents (B, D, E) are open-ended. In those, the next step depends on what was just discovered, so adaptive decomposition fits better.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The coordinator runs a sequential chain for a market-entry report: research regulations, then competitors, then consumer demographics, then logistics. Each step's prompt uses only the original topic, never earlier steps' outputs, and the report takes 40 minutes. What change best reduces latency without hurting quality?

options.text: Shorten each research step's instructions so that every step in the chain completes in less time than before.
Run the four independent research tasks in parallel, then combine their results in one synthesis step.
Combine all four research areas into a single prompt so that the model handles them in one long response.
Drop the two research areas that took longest in past runs and only cover them when a client asks for them.

questions.explanation: A sequential chain only makes sense when later steps depend on earlier outputs. Here the steps are independent, so running them in parallel (sectioning) and then aggregating cuts wall-clock time to roughly the longest task. Shorter instructions (A) may reduce quality and keep the needless serialization. One giant prompt (C) dilutes attention across four areas. Dropping research areas (D) reduces the report's coverage.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer runs several Claude Code investigations in the same repository each day: a flaky-test hunt, a payments refactor, and a dependency audit. Each evening she wants to pick up the payments investigation exactly where it left off, but 'claude --continue' often opens whichever session she used last. What should she do?

options.text: Copy the key findings into a notes file each evening and paste them into a brand-new session the next morning, so each day's work starts from a clean and focused context.
Run all three investigations in a single session so that --continue always brings back the right context.
Give each investigation a descriptive session name and resume the one she needs with --resume and its name.
Use --continue together with --fork-session so the most recent session is copied before she keeps working.

questions.explanation: --continue loads the most recent conversation in the directory, which is the wrong one when several investigations interleave. Naming sessions (for example with -n or /rename) and running 'claude --resume <name>' returns to a specific investigation with its context intact. Manual notes (A) work but throw away valid context she could simply resume. Mixing unrelated work in one session (B) pollutes context. Forking the most recent session (D) still starts from the wrong conversation.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. After a long session analyzing a monolith's order module, an engineer wants to compare two refactoring strategies, extracting a service versus modularizing in place. Each needs its own back-and-forth discussion that builds on the shared analysis. What is the best approach?

options.text: Discuss both strategies in the original session, alternating between them, so they share the same history.
Start two brand-new sessions and have each one redo the full analysis of the order module from scratch.
Finish one strategy completely in the original session, then use /compact and start on the other strategy.
Fork the analysis session twice, so each strategy gets its own branch starting from the same baseline.

questions.explanation: Forking creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history and then diverges, leaving the original unchanged. Two forks give each strategy the full shared analysis without the two discussions contaminating each other. Alternating in one session (A) mixes the strategies' reasoning. Redoing the analysis twice (B) wastes the work already done. Compacting between strategies (C) leaves the second one biased by the first and loses detail from the baseline.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Yesterday's named session mapped the notification subsystem in detail. Overnight, a teammate merged changes to three of the 40 files that session analyzed, and you know which three. Most of the analysis is still accurate. How should you continue today?

options.text: Resume the session and tell the agent which three files changed and how, so it re-reads only those files.
Resume the session without comment, since the agent will notice changed files the next time it reads them.
Start a new session and have the agent re-explore all 40 files so that its understanding is fully up to date.
Resume the session and ask the agent to re-read every file it analyzed before answering any new questions.

questions.explanation: When most prior context is still valid, resuming keeps that value. Telling the agent exactly which files changed lets it re-analyze just those instead of relying on stale tool results. Without that notice (B), the agent may answer from its earlier reads and never look at the files again. Full re-exploration (C) or re-reading everything (D) throws away 37 files of still-accurate analysis and costs time and context.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Two weeks ago a session analyzed the data access layer. Since then a large refactor replaced the ORM and moved most of the files that session read. You need to continue designing the caching strategy that session started. What is the most reliable way to proceed?

options.text: Resume the old session, since its record of the design discussion is the most complete source of context available.
Resume the old session and ask the agent to work out for itself which of its earlier conclusions are still valid, re-reading files only where it suspects something has changed.
Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of the still-relevant design decisions, then re-explore the new code.
Fork the old session so that the stale tool results stay in the original branch and the fork can start out clean.

questions.explanation: When most earlier tool results are stale, resuming pulls outdated file contents into context that can quietly mislead the agent. A fresh session seeded with a concise summary of the decisions that still matter, followed by exploration of the current code, is more reliable. Resuming as-is (A) or asking the agent to sort out what is stale (B) both leave misleading data in context. A fork (D) copies the full history, stale results included.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You forked an SDK session twice to try two refactoring approaches, and each fork's agent edits files in the same working directory. Afterwards the code contains a mix of both refactors, and tests fail. What explains this, and what should you do?

options.text: Forks should have isolated the files automatically, so this is a bug and the forks need to be recreated with fresh IDs.
Forks branch the conversation, not the filesystem, so give each branch its own working copy or use file checkpointing.
The original session was resumed while the forks were active, which merged the histories and their file edits.
The forks shared a session ID, so their edits were applied to both branches; fork from a new session ID instead.

questions.explanation: Forking copies the conversation history into a new session, but file edits are real and visible to any session working in the same directory. Exploring competing code changes safely needs filesystem isolation, such as a separate worktree or checkout per branch, or file checkpointing to revert changes. This is documented behavior, not a bug (A). Resuming the original (C) does not merge histories. Each fork gets its own session ID (D), so that is not the cause.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK service handles many customers at once, and customers often return hours later to continue a case. The service runs on several horizontally scaled hosts. Which TWO practices correctly restore each customer's own conversation? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Store each conversation's session ID against the customer's case and pass it to resume when they return.
Use the continue option so the SDK picks up the most recent session in the working directory each time.
Fork a new session for every incoming customer message so that each message runs in an isolated branch.
Use a session store adapter so transcripts are mirrored to shared storage that any host can resume from.
Keep a single long-running session for all customers so that the agent always has full context available.

questions.explanation: In a multi-user service you must resume by a specific session ID tracked per customer, and because session files are local to the host that wrote them, a session store adapter lets any host resume. The continue option (B) picks the most recent session in the directory, which would be another customer's in a busy service. Forking on every message (C) breaks continuity. One shared session (E) mixes customers' data and leaks private information.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A nightly SDK job that upgrades deprecated API calls across a large repo ended with an error_max_turns result after completing about 70% of the files. The session ID was captured, and nothing in the repo changed since. What is the best way to finish the work?

options.text: Start a new session with the original prompt and a higher turn limit so the agent redoes the upgrade cleanly.
Fork the session and have the fork review the 70% already upgraded before continuing with the remaining files.
Remove the turn limit entirely and rerun the job from the beginning so that it can never be cut off again.
Resume the captured session with a higher turn limit so the agent continues from where it stopped.

questions.explanation: Hitting a turn limit is a normal reason to resume: the session keeps everything the agent did and learned, and because the repo has not changed that context is still valid. Resuming with a higher limit lets it pick up the remaining 30%. Starting over (A, C) repeats the work already done, and removing all limits takes away the safety net. Forking to re-review (B) adds work with no benefit, since nothing has changed.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The web search subagent has two tools: search_web and find_references. Both are described only as "Finds relevant sources for a topic." Logs show the subagent often calls find_references, which queries the company's internal citation library, when the coordinator asked for current news coverage, and reports find nothing recent. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a system prompt rule telling the subagent to prefer search_web whenever the task mentions news or recent events
Lower the sampling temperature for the subagent so that it chooses between the two search tools more consistently
Rename find_references to search_internal_citations and rewrite both descriptions to state which corpus each covers and when to use the other
Have the coordinator call both search tools on every request, then deduplicate and merge all of the results before passing them to the subagent

questions.explanation: The root cause is two tools with near-identical names and descriptions, so the model has nothing to distinguish them; renaming and rewriting the descriptions to state each tool's corpus and when to use the alternative removes the overlap. A keyword rule in the system prompt (A) patches one phrasing and leaves the ambiguity in place for every other request. Temperature (B) makes the choice more repeatable, not more correct. Calling both tools for everything (D) doubles cost and noise without fixing selection.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your tool descriptions for get_customer and lookup_order were rewritten last month and are detailed and distinct. Since then, a new system prompt line was added: "Whenever the customer mentions their account, start by checking the account." Now the agent calls get_customer for messages like "where is the order on my account, #48213?" and never reaches lookup_order in that turn. What should you do first?

options.text: Add more detail and examples to the lookup_order description so that it outweighs the instruction in the system prompt
Reword the system prompt instruction so it no longer ties the word "account" to a tool, and describe the actual verification intent instead
Set tool_choice to force lookup_order on any turn where the user's message contains a sequence of digits that looks like an order number
Insert a preprocessing classifier that strips the word "account" from customer messages before they reach the agent

questions.explanation: The regression began with a keyword-sensitive system prompt instruction that creates an unintended association between the word "account" and get_customer, overriding good tool descriptions. Fixing the instruction addresses the cause directly. Making descriptions longer (A) fights the prompt instead of removing the conflict. Forcing a tool on a regex (C) and stripping words from customer input (D) are brittle workarounds that bypass the model's understanding and will misfire on other messages.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An internal MCP tool, query_service_logs, takes a service name, a time range, and a filter string. The agent frequently passes times like "yesterday afternoon," requests 30-day ranges that the backend rejects (the limit is 24 hours), and uses it to look up deploy history, which it does not contain. The current description is "Queries service logs." What change gives the biggest improvement?

options.text: Expand the description to specify the ISO 8601 UTC time format, the 24-hour range limit, a few example calls, and that deploy history lives in a different tool
Wrap the backend so it retries failed queries automatically with progressively shorter time ranges until one finally succeeds
Move the time format and range rules into the system prompt so that they apply to every tool the agent might call
Reduce the tool to a single free-text parameter and let the backend parse whatever time expressions the agent sends

questions.explanation: Each failure traces back to information the description never provided: input format, a boundary condition, and what the tool does not cover. Putting input formats, examples, limits, and scope boundaries in the description is the primary lever for correct tool use. Automatic shrinking retries (B) hide the error and return data for a range the user did not ask for. The system prompt (C) is the wrong place for tool-specific contracts. A single free-text parameter (D) makes the interface more ambiguous, not less.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document analysis subagent uses one tool, process_document(doc_id, mode), where mode is a free-text string such as "extract stats," "summarize," or "check quote." Outputs vary in shape from call to call, and the synthesis agent often cannot tell whether it received a summary or a list of extracted figures. What is the best redesign?

options.text: Keep the single tool but instruct the synthesis agent to infer the output type from the first line of whatever text it receives back
Add a mode enum to the existing tool and return all outputs as a single free-text field so the shape never varies
Have the subagent run all three modes on every document and return the combined output so nothing is ever missed
Split it into extract_statistics, summarize_document, and check_quote_against_source, each with its own defined input and output schema

questions.explanation: A generic tool with a free-text mode has no stable contract, which explains both the wrong-mode calls and the unpredictable output shapes. Purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts let the model choose by purpose and let downstream agents rely on a known structure. Making the consumer guess the output type (A) pushes the ambiguity downstream. An enum with one free-text output (B) fixes the input but leaves the output contract undefined. Running every mode (C) wastes work and tokens on outputs nobody requested.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are adding an issue_store_credit tool alongside the existing process_refund tool. Both move value back to the customer, and you expect the agent to confuse them. Which TWO elements should the new tool's description include to make selection reliable? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A statement of when to use store credit instead of process_refund, including the policy boundaries that separate the two
The accepted input formats, such as the credit amount and the order identifier, along with one or two example requests
An all-caps IMPORTANT prefix so the model weighs this description more heavily than the descriptions of other tools
A single short sentence, so the description stays as concise and scannable as the other tool descriptions in the agent's toolset
The names of the database tables and internal services that the tool writes to when it issues the credit

questions.explanation: Descriptions are the main signal the model uses to pick between similar tools, so they should say when to use this tool versus the alternative and what inputs it expects, with examples. Emphatic capitalization (C) does not add information and can cause overuse. A one-line description (D) is exactly what leads to unreliable selection among similar tools. Internal table and service names (E) are implementation details that do not help the model decide when or how to call the tool.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your team built two internal MCP servers, one for the ticket tracker and one for the wiki. Each exposes a tool named search with the description "Search for items." Engineers report that the agent searches the wiki when asked about open bugs and searches tickets when asked for design docs. What should you change?

options.text: Remove the wiki server from the agent's configuration and rely on engineers to paste any wiki content they need directly into the chat
