Rename the tools to search_tickets and search_wiki_pages and describe what each corpus contains and which questions it answers
Add a system prompt table that maps question types to servers and ask the agent to consult it before every search call
Configure tool_choice to alternate between the two search tools on consecutive turns so that both corpora get queried

questions.explanation: The servers are your own, so the cleanest fix is at the tool interface: names and descriptions that say which corpus each tool searches and what it is for. Removing a server (A) loses a capability to avoid a naming problem. A routing table in the system prompt (C) duplicates what the descriptions should carry and drifts out of sync. Alternating tool_choice (D) is arbitrary and guarantees wrong calls half the time.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document analysis subagent's read_paper tool returns only the first 20 pages of a PDF plus a next_page_token, but its description says "Returns the contents of a paper." The synthesis agent's reports confidently summarize conclusions sections that the subagent never actually read. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Raise the page limit to 200 pages so that nearly every paper fits in a single call to the read_paper tool
Ask the synthesis agent to add a standard disclaimer to every report noting that some of its sources may have been only partially read
Have the coordinator re-run the document analysis subagent whenever a report includes conclusions that look suspicious
Update the description to state the 20-page limit and how to use next_page_token, and include a truncated flag in the output

questions.explanation: The subagent does not know the tool truncates, because the description misstates the output. Documenting the limit and how to page, and flagging truncation in the result, lets the model fetch the rest when it needs it. A much larger page limit (A) floods the context and still fails for longer papers. A blanket disclaimer (B) admits the problem without fixing it. Rerunning on output that looks suspicious (C) relies on a judgment the coordinator cannot reliably make.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. process_refund returns {"error": "Operation failed"} for every failure. In logs, the agent retries refunds that failed because the purchase is outside the 90-day window, and tells customers there is "a technical issue" when the payment service was actually just slow. What change best enables correct recovery decisions?

options.text: Add a system prompt rule limiting the agent to two retries for any tool call that returns an error of any kind
Have the tool throw an exception on failure so the agent framework ends the conversation and opens a ticket
Return structured error metadata with an errorCategory such as transient or business, an isRetryable flag, and a readable description
Log the detailed failure reason on the server and keep the generic message so customers never see internal details

questions.explanation: A uniform error message hides the one fact the agent needs: whether the failure is transient and worth retrying or a policy violation that never will succeed. Structured metadata with a category, a retryable flag, and a description lets the agent retry the slow payment and explain the policy for the 90-day case. A blanket retry cap (A) still wastes retries on policy errors and gives up too early on transient ones. Ending the conversation (B) abandons recoverable cases. Keeping the generic message (D) leaves the agent as blind as before.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer asks for a $900 refund, but policy caps agent-issued refunds at $500. process_refund correctly rejects the request. What should the tool return so the agent handles this well?

options.text: A successful result with an empty body, so the agent does not treat the policy rejection as a malfunction
An isError result marked as a non-retryable business error, with a customer-friendly explanation of the $500 limit
An isError result marked as transient, so the agent tries the refund again later after the limit has reset
A successful result that silently issues $500 instead, with a note in the response explaining that the amount was reduced

questions.explanation: This is a business rule violation: retrying will never succeed, and the customer needs a clear explanation. Marking it non-retryable with a customer-friendly reason lets the agent explain the limit and offer escalation. An empty success (A) misleads the agent into telling the customer the refund went through. Marking it transient (C) invites pointless retries. Silently issuing a different amount (D) takes a financial action the customer did not agree to.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document search subagent's search_corpus tool returns an empty list both when the index service is unreachable and when a query legitimately matches nothing. During an outage, the final report stated that "no peer-reviewed studies exist" on the topic. How should the tool be changed?

options.text: Return an access-failure error when the index is unreachable, and a successful result with zero matches when nothing matches
Retry every empty result three times before returning, since an empty list most likely means the index is still warming up
Return a placeholder document saying "index unavailable" in the results list so the report shows the source was not reachable
Instruct the synthesis agent never to claim that something does not exist, and to say that results were inconclusive instead

questions.explanation: The tool conflates two different outcomes: a failed access, which needs a retry or escalation decision, and a valid empty result, which is real information. Returning an error for the outage and a success with zero matches for a real miss lets downstream agents reason correctly. Retrying every empty result (B) wastes calls on legitimate misses and assumes the cause. A fake document in the results (C) pollutes the data with something that is not a source. A prompt rule on the synthesis agent (D) suppresses valid negative findings too.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The web search subagent fetches about a dozen sources per task. Some fetches fail with short-lived 503 responses that usually succeed seconds later; a few fail because a site blocks automated access. Today every failure goes straight to the coordinator, which spends turns re-delegating. Which TWO behaviors should the subagent implement? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Retry transient failures such as 503s locally a bounded number of times before reporting anything to the coordinator
Report failures it could not resolve to the coordinator along with the partial results gathered and what was attempted
Treat any source that fails to load as a successful result with no content so the coordinator's workflow stays simple
Send every individual failure to the coordinator as soon as it happens so the coordinator keeps full control of retries
Abort the entire research task as soon as any source fails, so incomplete findings never reach the synthesis agent

questions.explanation: Transient failures are best absorbed locally where the context is, and only failures that cannot be resolved there should go up, together with partial results and what was tried, so the coordinator can decide what to do next. Marking failures as successful empty results (C) hides gaps in coverage. Escalating every failure immediately (D) is the current behavior that wastes coordinator turns. Aborting on any failure (E) throws away good results when recovery is possible.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. The agent calls an internal MCP tool, read_repo_file, to inspect a private repository. The tool returns HTTP 403 because the service account lacks access. The agent retries several times, then tries to clone the repo through Bash with other credentials it finds in environment variables. What should the tool return?

options.text: A transient error so the agent waits and tries again later, since access permissions can sometimes take time to propagate
An empty file listing, so the agent concludes there is nothing to read and continues with the rest of its task
The raw 403 response body from the source host, so the agent has the complete technical details of the failure
A permission error marked non-retryable that names the access that is missing, so the agent reports it instead of working around it

questions.explanation: Permission errors are neither transient nor fixable by the agent, so the response should say so explicitly and name what access is needed, which lets the agent stop and report to the engineer. Labeling it transient (A) encourages exactly the retry loop you observed. An empty listing (B) disguises an access failure as a real result. Raw response bodies (C) carry detail without an explicit category or retry signal, so the agent still has to guess, and it may keep looking for a workaround.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. lookup_order accepts a date filter. When the agent passes "03/04/2026" instead of the required YYYY-MM-DD, your MCP server raises a JSON-RPC protocol error, and the agent loop shows only a generic tool failure. The agent then gives up on the lookup. What change follows MCP guidance and lets the agent self-correct?

options.text: Have the server silently guess the intended date from the ambiguous string and return the matching orders anyway
Keep the protocol error but add the expected date format to the JSON-RPC error message so that it is recorded in the server logs
Return a tool result with isError set to true and a message stating the expected YYYY-MM-DD format and the value received
Remove the date filter entirely so the tool returns all of a customer's orders and the agent filters them itself

questions.explanation: Under MCP, input validation problems such as a wrongly formatted date are tool execution errors: they belong in the tool result with isError: true so the model sees actionable feedback and can retry with corrected parameters. Protocol errors (B) are meant for structural problems like unknown tools, and clients are less likely to surface them usefully to the model. Guessing an ambiguous date (A) can return the wrong orders. Removing the filter (D) gives up a useful capability and floods the context.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An internal deployment MCP tool reports failures as opaque codes like "ERR_4127" with no other text. When a branch name is wrong, the agent cannot tell what happened and usually asks the engineer to investigate. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Publish a table of every error code in the project's CLAUDE.md file so that the agent can look up the meaning of each code it sees
Have the tool retry with the default branch whenever it receives an unknown branch name from the agent
Return a readable message that explains the problem and the next step, such as calling list_branches to see valid names
Increase the tool's timeout so fewer calls fail and the agent sees error codes less often during deployments

questions.explanation: Error responses are part of the tool interface: a message that states what went wrong and how to correct it lets the agent recover on its own. A code table elsewhere (A) forces an extra lookup and drifts out of date. Silently switching to the default branch (B) deploys something the engineer did not ask for. A longer timeout (D) does nothing for a bad branch name, which is not a timing problem.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The pipeline sets tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_source_metadata"} so each run begins by extracting metadata. Because the same request options are reused for every turn of the loop, the agent keeps calling extract_source_metadata and never reaches the enrichment tools. What should you change?

options.text: Remove extract_source_metadata from the toolset after the first turn so the model has no way to call it again
Switch tool_choice to any for every turn so that the model can choose among all tools while still calling one
Force the metadata tool only on the first request, then send follow-up turns with tool_choice set to auto
Add a system prompt note telling the agent to call extract_source_metadata only once per research task

questions.explanation: Forced tool choice applies to the request it is set on, so it should be used to guarantee the first step, then relaxed in later turns so the model can proceed. Removing the tool mid-conversation (A) changes the toolset under the model and loses the ability to re-extract when needed. Using any on every turn (B) still forbids a final text answer, so the loop cannot end naturally. A prompt note (D) cannot override a forced tool_choice, which is why the loop is stuck.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The synthesis agent was given the web search tools "just in case." It now runs its own searches mid-synthesis, pulls in sources the research agents never vetted, and some report claims have no citation trail. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction asking the synthesis agent to use web search only rarely and to cite anything it finds
Keep the tools but log every synthesis-agent search so reviewers can audit the unvetted sources after each report
Give the synthesis agent a larger context window so it can hold all research findings without needing to search
Remove the web search tools from the synthesis agent so it works only from findings delivered by the coordinator

questions.explanation: Agents given tools outside their specialization tend to use them, which here bypasses the research agents' vetting and breaks citation provenance. Scoping the synthesis agent to the tools its role needs removes the failure mode. A prompt asking for restraint (A) is probabilistic and the tools remain available. Auditing after the fact (B) detects the problem without preventing it. Context size (C) is unrelated to why the agent chooses to search.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document analysis subagent has a general fetch_url tool. It sometimes fetches arbitrary web pages and pasted links from source documents, which brings unvetted content into the analysis. Its job is only to analyze documents in the team's approved corpus. What change best fits its role?

options.text: Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that accepts a corpus document ID and rejects anything outside the approved store
Keep fetch_url and add a description sentence asking the subagent to fetch only URLs that belong to the approved corpus
Route every fetch_url call through the coordinator for manual approval before the subagent is allowed to continue
Add a URL blocklist of known low-quality domains and let fetch_url continue to reach everything else on the web

questions.explanation: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained alternative that validates its input enforces the role boundary at the interface, not through hope. A description sentence (B) is guidance the model can still ignore. Coordinator approval on every fetch (C) adds round trips for the common legitimate case. A blocklist (D) inverts the requirement: the role calls for an allowlist of approved documents, not a list of exceptions.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Before generating boilerplate, the agent must call load_repo_conventions so generated code matches the repository's patterns. In about 15% of runs it skips straight to writing files. You call the Messages API directly. What is the most reliable way to guarantee the first call happens?

options.text: Set tool_choice to any on the first request so the model must call some tool before it can respond in text
Strengthen the system prompt with a numbered checklist that lists the load_repo_conventions call as the first mandatory step
Force tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "load_repo_conventions"} on the first request, then let later turns choose
Remove the file-writing tools until the model has called load_repo_conventions at least three times in the session

questions.explanation: When one specific tool must run first, forcing that named tool on the first request makes it deterministic, and later turns can return to normal selection. Using any (A) guarantees a tool call but not which one, so the model could still pick a write tool first. A stronger prompt (B) improves odds but remains probabilistic. Requiring three calls (D) is arbitrary and wastes turns.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. An extraction step reads each source and must record it with one of three tools: record_journal_article, record_news_item, or record_dataset. Which tool fits depends on the source. About 8% of the time the model replies with a prose summary instead of calling any tool, which breaks the pipeline. What should you set?

options.text: tool_choice auto, together with a stronger instruction in the user message to always respond by using a tool
tool_choice any, so the model must call one of the three tools but can still pick the one that fits the source
tool_choice forcing record_journal_article, then correcting misclassified records in a later cleanup pass
tool_choice none, then parsing the model's prose summary into the record format with a separate post-processing script

questions.explanation: The requirement is that some tool is always called while the model still decides which one, which is exactly what any guarantees. Auto (A) is what you have now and still allows text responses. Forcing one tool (C) removes the classification the step exists to do. Disabling tools (D) gives up structured output and replaces it with fragile parsing.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. To stop the agent from answering without checking data, someone set tool_choice to any for every turn. Now, when a customer writes "Thanks, that's all," the agent calls get_customer again instead of closing the conversation, and it cannot ask clarifying questions without first making a tool call. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add a no_op tool that the agent can call when it only wants to reply, while leaving tool_choice set to any
Force escalate_to_human whenever the customer's message is shorter than ten words, so short messages are handled
Keep any but append "you may also reply directly" to the system prompt so the agent knows it can choose text
Return tool_choice to auto, and enforce must-happen checks such as pre-refund verification in code

questions.explanation: Setting any on every turn forbids plain text responses, which a conversational agent needs for closing and clarifying. Auto restores normal behavior, and a hard requirement such as verifying before refunds is better enforced in code at the point where it matters. A no_op tool (A) works around the setting it should simply change. Escalating short messages (B) sends trivial goodbyes to humans. A prompt note (C) cannot override any, which prefills a tool call.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. You define a citation-formatting subagent in Claude Code with a name, description, and prompt, but you leave out the tools field. During runs it occasionally edits files and runs shell commands, even though its only job is to reformat a citation list it receives. What should you do?

options.text: Explicitly list only the tools this subagent needs in its tools field, because omitting the field inherits the available tool set
Add a line to its prompt saying it must never edit files or run commands, since the tools field is only advisory
Move the formatting work into the coordinator so that no subagent has to be defined for this narrow task
Run the subagent in plan mode so it can propose shell commands and edits without ever executing them

questions.explanation: In Claude Code, a subagent with no tools field inherits the tools available to subagents, so a narrow role ends up with broad capabilities. Listing only the needed tools scopes it correctly. A prompt prohibition (B) is probabilistic, and the tools field is an actual restriction, not advisory. Folding the work into the coordinator (C) gives up context isolation to avoid a one-line configuration fix. Plan mode (D) does not match the role, which needs no edit or shell capability at all.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Other teams have added tools to the support agent over time: it now has 16, including inventory administration and marketing email tools. Wrong-tool calls have risen with each addition. Some support cases do need to know whether an item is in stock. Which TWO changes should you make? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Remove tools that are unrelated to resolving support cases, such as the marketing email and inventory administration tools
Add a narrow, read-only check_stock tool for the frequent stock question instead of keeping the full inventory toolset
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that show the correct use of each of the 16 tools in typical cases
Set tool_choice to any so that the agent is always committed to calling one of its tools before it replies to the customer
Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to reason about which of the 16 tools fits the current request

questions.explanation: Too many tools increase decision complexity and degrade selection, so tools outside the role should go; the one recurring cross-role need is better served by a narrow, read-only tool than by the full admin toolset. Few-shot examples for all 16 tools (C) add tokens while keeping the oversized toolset. Forcing any (D) makes wrong calls more likely, not less. More output tokens (E) do not reduce the number of similar options the model must choose between.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Senior engineers on your team use a Jira MCP server with Claude Code and the productivity agent. A new hire clones the repository, but the Jira tools are missing from their sessions. You find the server was added with claude mcp add using the default scope on each senior engineer's machine. What is the right fix?

options.text: Ask the new hire to run the same claude mcp add command with --scope user so it applies to all of their projects
Add the Jira server to the project's .mcp.json and commit it, using environment variable references for credentials
Paste the Jira server's configuration into the project's CLAUDE.md so that Claude Code reads it at session start
Copy a senior engineer's ~/.claude.json file into the repository so that every developer automatically gets the same configuration

questions.explanation: The default scope is private to each developer and stored in their home directory, so it never reaches teammates; shared team tooling belongs in the project-scoped .mcp.json checked into version control. Having each person add it to their own user scope (A) works only by manual repetition and does not stay in sync. CLAUDE.md (C) holds instructions, not server configuration. Committing someone's ~/.claude.json (D) leaks personal settings and is not where Claude Code reads project servers.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer wants to try an experimental MCP server that indexes her personal notes across all of her projects. The team has a committed .mcp.json for shared servers. Where should she configure the notes server?

options.text: In the team's .mcp.json, with an entry name marking it as experimental so teammates know they can safely ignore it
In a new branch's .mcp.json that she keeps locally and rebases onto main whenever she starts new work
In her user-scoped configuration in ~/.claude.json, so it loads in all her projects without affecting the team
In the project's .claude/settings.json so that it is loaded only when she has that specific repository open

questions.explanation: Personal or experimental servers belong in user scope, which is stored in ~/.claude.json, applies to all of that user's projects, and is not shared. Adding it to the shared .mcp.json (A) pushes a personal server onto every teammate. A long-lived private branch (B) is a maintenance burden and still ties the server to one repository. The project's settings.json (D) is shared with the team and ties the server to one repository, which misses the cross-project requirement.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your team wants the productivity agent to read and comment on GitHub pull requests, and also to trigger the team's in-house release workflow, which uses an internal approval service. A teammate proposes writing custom MCP servers for both. What is the better plan?

options.text: Write a single custom server that wraps both GitHub and the release workflow so that all of the code stays in one place
Skip MCP for both and have the agent call GitHub and the release service directly through curl commands in Bash
Use custom servers for both, because a community server cannot be given descriptions that suit the team's needs
Use an existing GitHub MCP server for the standard integration and build a custom server only for the release workflow

questions.explanation: Standard integrations like GitHub already have maintained MCP servers, so building your own duplicates work and maintenance; custom servers are best reserved for team-specific workflows like the internal release process. One custom wrapper for both (A) still reimplements GitHub. Raw curl through Bash (B) loses typed tool interfaces and structured results. Writing both from scratch on the assumption that community servers are unsuitable (C) ignores that their tools already cover the standard workflow.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You connected an internal code-intelligence MCP server that resolves symbols across all of your services, including generated code and dependency versions. Engineers notice the agent still answers "who calls this API?" by grepping the current repository, missing callers in other services. The server's tool is described as "Code search." What should you do first?

options.text: Expand the MCP tool's description to explain its cross-repository symbol resolution and when to prefer it over grep
Remove Grep and Bash from the agent's toolset so the MCP server is the only way for the agent to search code at all
Force tool_choice to the MCP tool on every turn so that it is always used for any code-related question
Add a CLAUDE.md line telling the agent to stop using grep, since grep searches are less accurate than the server

questions.explanation: The model prefers the familiar built-in search because the MCP tool's description does not explain what it can do that grep cannot. Describing its capabilities and outputs is the first, highest-leverage fix. Removing Grep and Bash (B) breaks many legitimate local tasks. Forcing the tool on every turn (C) prevents other tool calls and final answers. A blanket prohibition (D) is too broad, since grep is still the right tool for local text searches.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. The support agent's MCP server exposes about 60 policy documents (return rules by region, warranty terms, and so on). To answer a policy question, the agent typically calls list_policies, then get_policy on several guesses before finding the right one, adding several turns per case. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Load all 60 policy documents into the system prompt so the agent never needs a tool call to read a policy
Raise the agent's maximum tool-call budget per case so it has room to keep guessing until it finds the right policy
Expose the policy catalog as MCP resources so the agent can see which documents exist before reading one
Replace get_policy with a tool that returns all policies at once whenever any single policy is requested

questions.explanation: MCP resources are designed to expose content catalogs, giving the agent visibility into what is available without exploratory tool calls. Putting every policy in the system prompt (A) bloats every request with content that is mostly irrelevant. A larger tool-call budget (B) pays for the guessing instead of eliminating it. Returning all policies on every call (D) floods the context and buries the relevant one.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The research system's agents use three MCP servers: one for academic search, one for news archives, and one for the internal document store, each configured in the agent's MCP settings. A teammate proposes building a proxy server that merges the three so the agent "can see all the tools at once." How should you respond?

options.text: Agree, because a client can connect to only one MCP server at a time, so a proxy is required to combine them
Decline, because the client discovers the tools of every configured server when it connects, so they are already available together
Agree, but run each server in a separate agent session and merge their outputs in the coordinator afterward
Decline, and instead list every tool from all three servers by name in the system prompt for the agent to reference

questions.explanation: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered when the client connects and are available to the agent together, so a merging proxy adds a component that solves nothing. The claim that only one server can be connected (A) is false. Separate sessions per server (C) fragments the work for no benefit. Listing tool names in the system prompt (D) duplicates what discovery already provides and goes stale.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are writing the committed .mcp.json for the team's shared MCP servers. One server needs an API token, and its base URL differs between engineers who use a local mock and those who use staging. Which TWO practices should you apply? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Reference the token as ${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN} so each engineer supplies it from their own environment rather than the file
Commit the token directly in the file, since the repository is private and every engineer on the team needs the same token value
Use ${API_BASE_URL:-https://staging.internal.example.com} so engineers can override the URL and others get a default
Store the token in the project's CLAUDE.md file so that Claude can read it and supply it to the server when it connects
Keep a separate .mcp.json in each engineer's home directory and remove the shared one from the repository

questions.explanation: Environment variable expansion lets a shared .mcp.json reference secrets without committing them, and the default syntax handles values that differ per machine. Committing a token (B) puts a secret in version control regardless of repository visibility. CLAUDE.md (D) is loaded into the model's context, which is the wrong place for a credential. Dropping the shared file (E) gives up the team-wide configuration the project scope exists for.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer asks the agent to find every place in a large TypeScript monorepo that calls the function calculateTaxTotal before the function's signature changes. The agent has Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, and Glob available. Which approach should it take first?

options.text: Use Glob with the pattern **/*.ts to list every TypeScript file, then Read each file to look for the function name
Use Grep to search file contents for calculateTaxTotal across the repository and review the matching locations
Read the file where calculateTaxTotal is defined and infer from its imports where else it is likely to be called
Use Edit to change the function signature right away and rely on later build errors to reveal all of the callers

questions.explanation: Finding callers is a content search, which is what Grep is for: it returns the files and lines that mention the function name. Globbing and reading every file (A) is slow and floods the context. A definition file's imports (C) say what it depends on, not who calls it. Editing first and relying on build errors (D) is risky and misses dynamic or untyped call sites.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A developer asks the agent to list all database migration files in a repository where migrations live in several service directories, each named with a timestamp and ending in _migration.sql. The agent has Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, and Glob available. Which tool fits best?

options.text: Grep for the word CREATE across the repository, since nearly every migration file contains at least one CREATE statement
Read the repository's top-level README to find out where the team documents the migration folders it uses
Glob with a pattern such as **/*_migration.sql to match the files by name at any directory depth
Use Bash to run the migrations in dry-run mode and capture the list of files that the migration runner loads

questions.explanation: Finding files by name or extension pattern is a path-matching job, which Glob handles directly, including recursive ** patterns across directories. Grep (A) searches contents, so it matches unrelated SQL and misses migrations without a CREATE. A README (B) may be outdated and is an indirect route. Running the migration tool (D) has side-effect risk and is far heavier than a filename match.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. The agent needs to change a timeout value in one stanza of a generated YAML file that contains 40 byte-identical stanzas, differing only in their position. Edit keeps failing because the text it targets is not unique, and replace_all would change every stanza. What should the agent do?

options.text: Retry Edit with the same old_string several times, since the uniqueness check sometimes succeeds on a later attempt
Use Edit with replace_all set to true and then manually revert the other 39 stanzas with additional Edit calls
Ask the engineer to add unique comments to every stanza in the generator before attempting any change to the file
Read the full file, then Write the complete updated content with the change applied to the intended stanza only

questions.explanation: When no unique anchor text exists, reading the whole file and writing back the complete modified content is the reliable fallback for a targeted change. Repeating the same Edit (A) fails deterministically for the same reason. replace_all followed by reverting 39 stanzas (B) is error-prone and multiplies the edits. Changing the generator (C) may be worthwhile later, but it blocks a simple change on unrelated work.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Asked to explain how authentication works in an unfamiliar 3,000-file service, the agent starts reading files alphabetically and runs out of context before reaching the auth code. What approach should it use instead?

options.text: Use Grep to find entry points such as the login route or auth middleware, then Read those files and follow imports
Read every file in the src directory first so that the agent has complete context before attempting an explanation
Use Glob to list all files, then Read the largest ones first, since they are most likely to contain the core logic
Ask the engineer to paste the relevant files into the chat, since agents cannot explore large codebases reliably

questions.explanation: Building understanding incrementally, by locating entry points with a content search and then reading along imports, spends context only on relevant code. Reading everything upfront (B) is the failure you already saw. File size (C) is a poor proxy for relevance. Handing the exploration back to the engineer (D) gives up a task the agent is well suited to when it searches first.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer asks which modules use the payments client. The agent greps for createPaymentsClient and finds only three call sites, but the engineer knows there are more. It turns out a shared module re-exports the function as makeClient and getPayments, and most code imports those names. How should the agent trace usage reliably?

options.text: Grep only for the import path of the shared module, because every consumer must import it from that same file
First identify every name the wrapper module exports for the function, then Grep the codebase for each of those names
Read every file that imports anything from the shared module and look for any calls that might reach the client
Use Glob to find files whose names include payment, since modules that use the client are likely to be named that way

questions.explanation: When wrapper modules re-export a function under other names, a search for the original name misses most callers; finding all exported aliases first and then searching for each covers every route. Searching for the import path (A) misses consumers that import through other re-exporting modules or relative paths. Reading every importer (C) is expensive and still relies on spotting renamed calls by eye. Filenames (D) are an unreliable proxy for usage.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are reviewing how the agent chooses built-in tools in recent sessions. Which TWO choices were correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Using Edit to change a single function's return type in one file, with enough surrounding text to make the match unique
Using Write to change one line in a 2,000-line configuration file by regenerating the entire file from memory in one pass
Using Glob to find every file that contains a TODO comment so the engineer can review the outstanding work
Using Grep to locate where the error message "invoice total mismatch" is defined after a user reported seeing it
Using Read on the repository root directory to search all source files for references to a deprecated API

questions.explanation: Edit is meant for targeted changes anchored on unique text, and Grep is the right way to find where a specific string appears in code. Regenerating a large file with Write for a one-line change (B) risks dropping or altering unrelated content. Glob matches file paths, not file contents, so it cannot find TODO comments (C). Read loads a file's contents; it does not search across a repository (E).

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Engineers notice that when the agent makes small fixes, it often rewrites entire large files with Write, and diffs occasionally show unrelated lines changed or comments lost. What should you change in how the agent modifies files?

options.text: Require the agent to run a formatter after every Write, so that unrelated differences are normalized away before review
Add a pre-commit hook that rejects any commit touching more than 20 lines, so oversized rewrites never get merged
Increase the agent's output token limit so that it can always reproduce a whole file accurately whenever it rewrites one
Have the agent use Edit with unique anchor text for targeted changes, and reserve Write for new files or full rewrites

questions.explanation: The problem is the tool choice: Write replaces the whole file, so every small fix risks regenerating unrelated content, while Edit changes only the matched text. A formatter (A) cannot restore lost comments or altered logic. More output tokens (C) still asks the model to reproduce content it should not touch. A line-count hook (B) blocks legitimate large changes and does not stop the agent from making the risky rewrite in the first place.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A new engineer reports that Claude Code ignores the team's error-handling and logging conventions, while the tech lead says Claude always follows them on her machine. You find that the conventions live in the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What is the best fix?

options.text: Ask the new engineer to copy the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md into their own home directory so both machines match.
Move the conventions into the repository's project-level CLAUDE.md and commit it so every clone receives them.
Have each engineer paste the conventions at the start of a session and rely on auto memory to retain them.
Add the conventions to the repository README and tell Claude in each prompt to read the README first.

questions.explanation: The root cause is scope: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to the user who owns it and is never shared through version control. Moving the conventions into the project CLAUDE.md and committing it gives every engineer the same instructions on clone or pull. Copying the home-directory file works for one person but creates drifting private copies that nobody maintains. Pasting conventions each session and relying on auto memory is manual and per-machine, and pointing Claude at a README in every prompt depends on people remembering to do it.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your monorepo has a shared standards/ directory containing pci-handling.md, accessibility.md, graphql-schema.md and data-retention.md. The payments package needs only the PCI and data-retention guidance, and the web package needs only the accessibility and GraphQL guidance. Each package's maintainers know best which standards apply to their code. How should you provide this guidance to Claude Code?

options.text: Concatenate all four standards files into the root CLAUDE.md so every package has the complete set available.
Copy the relevant standards text into each package's CLAUDE.md and update the copies whenever the shared files change.
Package each standards file as a skill and rely on Claude to invoke the right ones when working in each package.
Have each package's CLAUDE.md @import only the standards files its maintainers judge relevant to that package.

questions.explanation: The @import syntax lets each package's CLAUDE.md pull in exactly the shared files its maintainers select, so the standards stay single-sourced and each package gets only what applies. Putting all four files in the root CLAUDE.md loads irrelevant guidance everywhere. Copying text into each package creates duplicates that drift from the shared originals. Skills load on invocation, so standards that should always apply in a package would depend on Claude or a developer choosing to load them.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering testing, API conventions, deployment and security. Four teams edit it, which causes frequent merge conflicts, and nobody can tell which team owns which section. What restructuring best addresses this?

options.text: Split it into focused topic files in .claude/rules/, such as testing.md, api-conventions.md and deployment.md, each owned by a team.
Move each team's section into its members' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files so the teams stop editing a shared file.
Keep the single file but add a table of contents and an ownership comment at the top of every section.
Convert every section into a slash command so each team can load its own guidance whenever it remembers to.

questions.explanation: .claude/rules/ exists as the modular alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md: one topic per file gives clear ownership and removes most merge conflicts while the content still reaches every session. Teams can later add paths frontmatter to topic files that only matter for certain files. Moving sections into home directories stops them from being shared at all. A table of contents does not fix the conflicts or ownership problem, and slash commands turn always-needed standards into something that loads only when someone remembers to invoke it.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Engineers using Claude Code to explore a large legacy repository report inconsistent behavior: some sessions follow the billing module's conventions and others do not. Some engineers launch Claude from the repository root and others from services/billing/. Before rewriting any instructions, what should you do first?

options.text: Duplicate the billing conventions into the root CLAUDE.md so they load no matter where a session starts.
Require everyone to launch from the repository root and add a reminder about it to the README.
Run /memory (and /context) in sessions started from each location to see which instruction files are in effect.
Rewrite the billing conventions with stronger wording such as MUST and NEVER so Claude weighs them more heavily.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent behavior across sessions is a configuration-hierarchy question, so the first step is to verify which memory files each session actually has, which /memory and /context show. CLAUDE.md files above the launch directory load at startup while subdirectory files load on demand, so launch location can plausibly explain the difference. Duplicating content or changing launch habits treats a cause you have not confirmed. Stronger wording assumes the file is loaded and being ignored, which may not be true.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A tech lead wants every engineer's Claude Code sessions to follow the team's testing conventions. She also wants Claude to give her terse responses in every project she works on, a preference she does not want to impose on teammates. Which TWO placements meet both goals? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Put the testing conventions in the repository's CLAUDE.md and commit it to version control.
Put the testing conventions in her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ask each teammate to do the same.
Add the terse-response preference to the project CLAUDE.md under an "Optional" heading.
Put the terse-response preference in her own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file.
Store both items in a committed CLAUDE.local.md file at the repository root.

questions.explanation: Shared team conventions belong in the project CLAUDE.md, which reaches everyone through version control. A personal preference that should apply across all of her projects belongs in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which only she loads. Asking teammates to maintain user-level copies of team conventions invites drift. Putting a personal preference in the project file imposes it on everyone regardless of the heading, and CLAUDE.local.md is meant to be gitignored and only covers one project, so committing it defeats both purposes.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your CLAUDE.md contains the line "Follow the API style guide in docs/api-style.md." Claude follows the style guide in some sessions and ignores it in others. What change makes the guide's content reliably available?

options.text: Move the sentence to the top of CLAUDE.md and mark it as critical so Claude is more likely to open the file.
Replace the prose reference with an @docs/api-style.md import so the file's content loads with CLAUDE.md.
Create a skill named api-style that contains the guide and tell developers to invoke it before API work.
Paste the full guide into each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it loads for everyone in every project.

questions.explanation: A prose pointer only works when Claude decides to open the file, which explains the inconsistency. An @path import expands the referenced file into context alongside the CLAUDE.md that imports it, so it is always present. Moving or emphasizing the sentence still leaves loading to Claude's judgment. A skill depends on someone invoking it, and user-level copies are not shared, drift over time, and load in unrelated projects.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Early in a long session a developer told Claude, "Use pnpm, never npm, in this repo." After the conversation was compacted, Claude started running npm commands again. The rule applies to all work in the repository. What is the most durable fix?

options.text: Repeat the instruction in chat after every compaction and ask Claude to confirm it before continuing.
Turn off auto-compaction for the repository so earlier conversation turns are never summarized.
Add the rule to the project CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code re-reads from disk after compaction.
Create a /pnpm slash command that restates the rule and ask developers to run it periodically.

questions.explanation: Instructions given only in conversation can be lost when the conversation is summarized, while the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk and re-injected after compaction. A repository-wide rule therefore belongs in CLAUDE.md. Repeating it manually or running a reminder command relies on people noticing the regression. Disabling compaction trades the problem for context exhaustion in long sessions and still leaves the rule out of every new session.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Engineers use a project skill, /map-dependencies, that scans hundreds of files and produces long intermediate output before returning a short dependency summary. After running it, the main session is cluttered and later answers degrade. The skill's instructions are self-contained. What change best addresses this?

options.text: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter so it runs in an isolated subagent and returns only its result.
Add a final step telling Claude to summarize the scan and ignore the intermediate output for the rest of the session.
Move the skill's instructions into CLAUDE.md so the dependency analysis runs as part of every session's startup.
Ask engineers to run /compact immediately after each invocation to shrink the leftover analysis output.

questions.explanation: context: fork runs the skill in a separate subagent context, so the verbose scanning stays out of the main conversation and only the result comes back. That fits here because the skill's instructions stand on their own. Telling Claude to ignore output does not remove it from context. Moving the procedure into CLAUDE.md would load it into every session, and routine /compact after each run is a manual workaround that also summarizes away useful earlier context.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team's /triage-bug skill needs a ticket ID to fetch the reproduction steps. Developers often type /triage-bug with no argument, and Claude then guesses which ticket they mean. What is the most direct improvement?

options.text: Add a note to CLAUDE.md reminding developers that /triage-bug requires a ticket ID when it is used.
Split the skill into one skill per component so each version can infer the ticket from the component.
Add context: fork so the skill runs in isolation and cannot pick up the wrong ticket from conversation history.
Add argument-hint: [ticket-id] to the frontmatter and reference $ARGUMENTS in the skill body.

questions.explanation: argument-hint shows the expected parameter when a developer types the command, and $ARGUMENTS passes the value into the skill body, which can also tell Claude to ask for the ID when none is supplied. This fixes the missing-parameter problem at the point of invocation. A CLAUDE.md note is easy to overlook when typing a command. Splitting by component does not supply a ticket ID, and context: fork changes isolation, not argument handling.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team maintains a project skill, /release-notes, in .claude/skills/. You want a version that formats notes for your personal weekly update, but you still use the team version for official releases and must not change teammates' behavior. What should you do?

options.text: Edit .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md locally with your changes and be careful never to commit them.
Create a personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name, like /my-release-notes.
Create ~/.claude/skills/release-notes/ with the same name so your version overrides the team's version.
Add a branch to the team skill that switches to your format whenever your username is detected.

questions.explanation: A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ is visible only to you, and giving it a distinct name keeps both versions available. A personal skill with the same name takes precedence over the project skill, so you would lose access to the team version you still need. Uncommitted local edits to a tracked file are fragile and easy to commit by accident. Adding user-specific logic to the shared skill changes a team asset for one person's preference.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your CLAUDE.md contains (1) a 70-line runbook for rotating feature-flag configuration, used about twice a month, and (2) the rule that all code must pass the repository's lint command before commit. Context usage is high and the runbook is rarely relevant. Which TWO changes are most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Move the lint rule into a skill so it loads only when someone types the skill's command.
Move the runbook into a skill so its full content loads only when that workflow is invoked.
Move both items into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so that they stop counting against the project's own context budget.
Keep the runbook in CLAUDE.md but compress it into a single dense paragraph of instructions.
Keep the lint rule in CLAUDE.md because it is a universal standard that should always be loaded.

questions.explanation: Skills suit task-specific, on-demand workflows: the runbook's full content then loads only when it is needed. CLAUDE.md suits always-applicable standards such as the lint requirement, which should be present in every session. Making the lint rule a skill means it might not be loaded when code is committed. User-level files still load into context and are not shared with the team, and compressing the runbook keeps a rarely used procedure in every session while making it harder to follow.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A project skill, /commit-split, stages and commits changes as several logical commits. Each git add and git commit triggers a permission prompt, so the workflow keeps stalling. You want those specific commands approved while the skill runs, without loosening permissions elsewhere. What should you do?

options.text: Start sessions with --dangerously-skip-permissions whenever developers plan to run the skill.
Add a broad Bash allow rule to the project's settings so all shell commands run without prompts.
Add allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) to the skill's frontmatter.
Add context: fork so the skill's commands run in a subagent that does not need approval.

questions.explanation: allowed-tools in skill frontmatter pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill, so the two git commands run without prompts while other tools stay under the normal permission rules. Skipping permissions entirely removes every safeguard for the whole session. A broad Bash allow rule approves all shell commands everywhere, not just this workflow. A forked subagent is still governed by permissions, so context: fork does not remove the prompts.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A /scaffold-module skill should only create new files from templates. During testing it occasionally ran shell commands that deleted and regenerated directories. You need shell use blocked while the skill is active, not merely discouraged. What is the best approach?

options.text: List Bash under disallowed-tools in the skill's frontmatter so the tool is removed while the skill runs.
Add a sentence to the skill body stating that this skill must never run shell commands under any circumstances.
Add a CLAUDE.md rule saying that scaffolding work should avoid deleting directories with shell commands.
Add context: fork so any shell commands the skill runs happen in a subagent isolated from the main session.

questions.explanation: disallowed-tools removes the listed tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active, which is a configuration guarantee rather than a request. Instructions in the skill body or CLAUDE.md are probabilistic, and the stem requires a block. context: fork isolates context, not capability, so destructive commands could still run in the subagent. Note that allowed-tools would not help here, because it pre-approves tools without restricting the others.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A developer writes a /decision-log skill that summarizes the architecture decisions made earlier in the current conversation. Because the skill can take a while, they added context: fork. Its summaries now miss every decision that was discussed. What is the cause and the fix?

options.text: The skill's description is too short; expand it so Claude knows which kinds of decisions to look for.
Forked skills get a smaller context window; split the summary into several smaller skill invocations.
The skill needs an argument-hint so the developer can pass the decision topics in as parameters.
A forked skill does not see the conversation history; remove context: fork from this skill.

questions.explanation: With context: fork, the skill content becomes the prompt for a new subagent that does not receive the main conversation's history, so a skill whose task depends on that history has nothing to summarize. Removing the fork lets the skill run in the main context where the decisions live. The description affects when the skill is selected, not what context it sees. Splitting invocations or passing topics as arguments still leaves the subagent without the discussion itself.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team split CLAUDE.md into 14 files in .claude/rules/. Every session, including backend-only work, still loads the iOS and Android rule files, which wastes context. What change fixes this?

options.text: Move the mobile rule files out of the repository into ~/.claude/rules/ on mobile engineers' machines.
Add paths frontmatter with globs for the mobile source directories to the mobile rule files.
Merge the mobile rules back into a single mobile.md file so they load as one smaller unit.
Reference the mobile rules as @imports from the root CLAUDE.md so they load only when needed.

questions.explanation: Rule files without a paths field load unconditionally, so splitting alone does not reduce context. Adding paths globs makes each mobile rule load only when Claude works with matching files. Moving the rules to some users' home directories removes them from the shared project and from anyone else who touches mobile code. Merging files does not change when they load, and @imports load together with the CLAUDE.md that references them, so they are not lazy.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Each service in your monorepo keeps SQL migrations in its own folder, such as services/billing/migrations/ and services/search/migrations/, and new services are added regularly. You are writing .claude/rules/migrations.md, whose conventions must apply to every service's migration files, including future services, and to no other files. Which paths value fits best?

options.text: paths: ["migrations/*.sql"]
paths: ["services/billing/migrations/*.sql", "services/search/migrations/*.sql"]
paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"]
paths: ["**/*.sql"]

questions.explanation: The ** prefix matches a migrations folder at any depth, so the rule covers every current and future service without edits. A pattern with no directory wildcard is relative to the project root, so migrations/*.sql only matches a top-level migrations folder. Enumerating each service works today but must be updated for every new service. **/*.sql is too broad because it also matches seed data, queries and other SQL files that are not migrations.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You created .claude/rules/graphql.md with paths: ["**/*.graphql"]. Before opening any files, an engineer asks Claude how the team names GraphQL mutations, and Claude's answer ignores the rule. Later, while editing a schema file, Claude follows the rule. What explains this?

options.text: This is expected: a path-scoped rule loads once Claude reads or edits a matching file, and none had been touched yet.
The glob does not match nested folders; it should be changed to "*.graphql" so it matches from the root down.
Path-scoped rules load only in plan mode, so the engineer should switch to plan mode before asking.
Path-scoped rules load only for file edits, never for reads, so Claude must be editing a matching file.

questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules are conditional: they load when Claude reads, writes or edits a file matching the glob, which is how they save context. A general question asked before any matching file is touched will not have the rule loaded; if the guidance must always be present, it should have no paths field. The existing **/*.graphql already matches nested files, and *.graphql would only match the root. Plan mode has nothing to do with rule loading, and reads of matching files do trigger it.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your API handler conventions apply to files under src/api/ and to older handlers under legacy/handlers/. A colleague created two identical rule files, one scoped to each directory, and the two have already drifted apart. What is the best fix?

options.text: Delete both rule files and put the conventions in a CLAUDE.md at the repository root instead.
Keep both files and add a CI check that diffs them and fails the build when they diverge.
Move legacy/handlers/ into src/api/ so a single directory-level CLAUDE.md can cover both locations.
Keep one rule file whose paths list includes both "src/api/**/*" and "legacy/handlers/**/*".

questions.explanation: A rule's paths field accepts multiple glob patterns, so one file can scope the same conventions to both locations and there is nothing left to drift. Moving the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md loads them in every session, including work that never touches handlers. A diff check polices duplication instead of removing it. Relocating code to fit the configuration is a disruptive change made for the wrong reason.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You are deciding what stays in the always-loaded root CLAUDE.md and what moves into path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/. Which TWO conventions are the best candidates for path-scoped rules? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use pnpm for every install and script command in the repository.
Storybook conventions that apply only to *.stories.tsx files across many packages.
Write every commit message in the Conventional Commits format.
Conventions for Alembic migration scripts found under any alembic/versions/ folder.
Briefly explain the plan before making any change that spans several files.

questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules fit conventions tied to particular file types or locations, especially ones spread across the codebase, such as Storybook stories and Alembic migrations. Those load only when Claude touches matching files, which keeps them out of unrelated sessions. Package-manager choice, commit message format and working style apply to all work regardless of which files are open. Those belong in the always-loaded CLAUDE.md.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A developer wants Claude to follow her personal docstring style whenever it edits Python files, in every repository she works on. Her teammates use different styles, and the guidance is irrelevant when she works on non-Python files. Where should this guidance live?

options.text: In each repository's .claude/rules/ directory, committed with a paths glob that matches Python files.
In her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so that it loads in every session across all of her projects.
In a file under ~/.claude/rules/ with paths: ["**/*.py"] in its frontmatter.
In a CLAUDE.local.md file that she recreates at the root of each repository she works in.

questions.explanation: User-level rules in ~/.claude/rules/ apply to every project on her machine without being shared, and paths frontmatter makes the rule load only when she works on Python files. Committing the rule to each repository imposes her style on teammates. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal but loads in every session, including non-Python work. CLAUDE.local.md is per project and always loaded, so she would be maintaining copies that still load when they are irrelevant.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A production error report includes a stack trace pointing to parseInvoiceDate() in one file, where a missing null check on an optional field throws an exception. The fix is clear and the function already has tests. How should you proceed?

options.text: Enter plan mode so Claude can survey all other date-parsing code before proposing any change.
Use direct execution: ask Claude to add the null check and a regression test, then run the tests.
Delegate to the Explore subagent to map every caller of the function before anything is edited.
Ask Claude to interview you about date-handling requirements before it touches the function.

questions.explanation: This is a well-scoped, single-file fix with a clear stack trace, which is exactly where direct execution fits; a regression test and a test run supply the verification. Plan mode adds overhead that pays off when the approach is uncertain or many files change, which is not the case here. Mapping every caller or running a requirements interview solves problems this bug does not have. If you could describe the diff in one sentence, planning is usually unnecessary.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You need to replace a deprecated HTTP client library across about 50 files. Usage varies: some files rely on interceptors, some on retries and some on streaming responses, and the new library handles each differently. Which workflow fits best?

options.text: Plan the migration in plan mode, then approve the plan and let Claude implement it, verifying with tests.
Stay in plan mode for the entire migration so that every individual file change is re-planned before editing.
Skip planning and use direct execution, since the new library's documentation already defines the target API.
Plan in plan mode, then discard the plan and start a fresh direct session so implementation is unbiased.

questions.explanation: A migration with several usage patterns across dozens of files benefits from investigation and design first, and once the approach is agreed the work is execution. Plan mode for the investigation followed by direct implementation of the approved plan combines both strengths. Re-planning every file adds overhead after the design is settled. Skipping planning ignores that each usage pattern needs its own decision, and discarding the plan throws away the analysis you just paid for.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You must add real-time order-status updates to an existing app. The options are WebSockets through the existing API gateway, server-sent events behind the CDN, or a managed pub/sub service, and each has different infrastructure requirements. Nothing has been built yet. What should you do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to implement WebSockets directly, since it is the most common choice, and revisit it later if needed.
Have Claude build small prototypes of all three in direct execution and keep whichever passes tests first.
Record the choice in CLAUDE.md as an open question so Claude can weigh it during future sessions.
Use plan mode so Claude explores the gateway, CDN and deployment setup and compares the options before coding.

questions.explanation: Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure implications is an architectural decision, which is what plan mode is for: Claude reads the existing setup and proposes a design before any code is written. Defaulting to the most common option risks rework if it does not fit the gateway or CDN. Building three prototypes is expensive, and passing tests first says nothing about infrastructure fit. Noting an open question in CLAUDE.md defers the decision instead of making it.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer asks Claude Code to find every place a legacy billing flag is read, then redesign the flag handling, then implement the redesign. The discovery phase reads hundreds of files, and by the implementation phase Claude has lost track of earlier decisions because its context is nearly exhausted. What change best prevents this?

options.text: Ask Claude to read files in larger batches so the discovery phase finishes in fewer turns.
Run /compact before discovery begins so the session starts with as much free context as possible.
Delegate discovery to the Explore subagent so only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Split the work into three separate sessions with no shared notes so that every phase starts clean.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent does the verbose searching in its own context and returns a summary, so the main conversation keeps room for the redesign and implementation decisions. Reading in larger batches puts the same volume into context. Compacting before discovery frees little, because the discovery output is what fills the window. Separate sessions without shared notes lose the findings that later phases depend on.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. In plan mode, Claude proposes a plan for reworking the account settings API. While reviewing it, you notice that it removes a v1 endpoint that mobile clients still call. What should you do?

options.text: Approve the plan and ask Claude to restore the v1 endpoint once the implementation is complete.
Keep planning: tell Claude the v1 endpoint must stay backward compatible, then review the revision.
Reject the plan, leave plan mode, and implement the entire change yourself without Claude.
Approve the plan and add a CLAUDE.md note about v1 compatibility so future sessions avoid it.

questions.explanation: Plan mode exists so that flaws are caught before code changes, so the right move is to keep planning and give Claude the missing constraint, then review the revised plan. Approving a plan you know is wrong and repairing it afterward creates the rework plan mode is meant to prevent. Abandoning Claude over one correctable gap discards the useful analysis. A CLAUDE.md note helps future sessions but lets this implementation break mobile clients.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. A platform engineer wants Claude Code to study an unfamiliar, business-critical deployment repository and propose how to add canary releases. She must be confident that no source files change while Claude investigates. What is the best approach?

options.text: Start in plan mode so Claude can read and analyze the repository while edits stay blocked until she approves a plan.
Use direct execution and put "do not modify any files" at the top of the prompt so Claude knows the rule.
Use direct execution and reject any proposed edit that appears before the design discussion has finished.
Copy the repository to a scratch folder and let Claude edit freely there before porting changes back.

questions.explanation: Plan mode is designed for safe exploration: Claude researches and proposes changes, and edits to source stay blocked until the plan is approved. A prompt instruction is probabilistic, which does not meet her need for confidence. Rejecting edits one by one depends on her catching every prompt. A scratch copy adds a porting step and still lets Claude start editing before any design exists.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Which TWO of these tasks most warrant starting in plan mode rather than direct execution? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Renaming a misspelled local variable inside a single function.
Adding a conditional that rejects end dates earlier than start dates in one existing validator function.
Splitting a shared auth module used by 12 services into separate token and session packages.
Adding a log line that records the request ID in an existing error handler.
Changing the caching strategy in code you have never worked in, where several designs seem viable.

questions.explanation: Plan mode pays off for large multi-file changes with architectural impact, like splitting a widely shared module, and when you are unfamiliar with the code and several approaches are valid, like the caching change. In both, exploring before editing prevents costly rework. Renaming a variable, adding one validation conditional and adding a log line are well-scoped changes you could describe in one sentence. Those suit direct execution.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You asked Claude to convert legacy log lines into structured JSON events. Your prose specification ("extract the timestamp, level and component; put the rest in message") yields a different field split on each run, especially for lines that contain nested brackets. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Rewrite the specification in more detailed prose, defining each field in its own paragraph.
Ask Claude to restate its interpretation of the specification before each conversion run.
Give two or three real log lines with the exact JSON expected, including a nested-bracket line.
Ask Claude to emit the fields in alphabetical order and to add no keys beyond the four that are listed.

questions.explanation: When prose is interpreted inconsistently, a few concrete input/output pairs are the clearest way to pin down the transformation, and including the nested-bracket case targets exactly where runs diverge. More prose tends to add more room for interpretation. Having Claude restate its understanding does not anchor it to the output you want. Ordering and key constraints control formatting, not how the line is split into fields.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You are implementing a shipping-cost calculator with tiered weights, regional surcharges, free-shipping thresholds, and a requirement that 10,000 quotes compute in under one second. Earlier attempts kept breaking existing cases while fixing new ones. Which workflow is most effective?

options.text: Write tests first for the tiers, edge cases and performance budget, then iterate by sharing failures.
Have Claude implement the full calculator first, then write tests that match whatever it produced.
Describe every pricing rule in one long prompt and ask Claude to double-check its own logic at the end.
Implement one tier per session and manually spot-check a few quotes before moving to the next tier.

questions.explanation: Test-driven iteration fits rule-heavy logic with regressions: a suite covering expected behavior, edge cases and the performance requirement gives Claude an objective signal, and sharing failures guides each fix without breaking earlier cases. Writing tests after implementation just encodes whatever bugs exist. Self-checking in one long prompt provides no external verification. Manual spot-checks across sessions are slow and miss regressions in tiers already done.

questions.question: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. An engineer who is new to distributed systems asks Claude Code to add caching in front of a slow inventory service. The requirements are vague, and she is not sure which questions matter. What is the best first step?

options.text: Ask Claude to implement a standard read-through cache now and refine it after it reaches production.
Enter plan mode and ask Claude to choose the most popular caching library for the current stack.
Write a test suite now based on her current assumptions, then have Claude implement against it.
Have Claude interview her on staleness, invalidation and failure modes before building.

questions.explanation: In an unfamiliar domain, the interview pattern has Claude surface considerations she may not have anticipated, such as how stale data can be, what invalidates entries, and what happens when the cache or service fails. Shipping a default cache first defers those decisions to production incidents. Picking a library answers a narrower question than the design ones. Tests written from untested assumptions would lock in the gaps the interview is meant to reveal.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. A data-migration script that Claude wrote works for most rows, but it writes the string "None" when middle_name is null and crashes when signup_date is null. You already said "handle nulls correctly" once, with no improvement. What should you do next?

options.text: Repeat the request with stronger wording, asking Claude to be very careful about every possible null value it might encounter.
Give specific test cases: input rows with null middle_name and signup_date plus the exact expected output.
Ask Claude to wrap the migration in a try/except block that skips any row that raises an error.
Switch to plan mode and ask Claude to redesign the migration script's architecture from scratch.

questions.explanation: Concrete test cases with example input and expected output state precisely what correct null handling means for each field, which a general instruction did not. Stronger wording repeats the vague request. Skipping rows that raise errors hides the bug and silently drops data. Redesigning the whole script is out of proportion to two specific edge cases.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Review of a Claude-generated feature found three problems: the order schema stores amounts as floats, the validator rounds those floats, and the serializer formats them for display. Separately, there is a help-text typo on an unrelated page. How should you communicate these to Claude?

options.text: Report the four issues one at a time, waiting for each fix before mentioning the next one.
Send all four in one message and ask Claude to fix everything together in a single pass.
Describe the three amount issues together in one detailed message, and handle the typo on its own.
Fix the schema yourself, then ask Claude to update the validator, the serializer and the typo afterward.

questions.explanation: The amount issues interact: changing the schema's type changes what the validator and serializer must do, so they need to be addressed together in one detailed message. The typo is independent and is simplest to handle separately. Fixing the interacting issues one at a time risks each fix being undone by the next. Bundling the unrelated typo into the coordinated change adds noise, and fixing the schema by hand splits one coordinated change across two actors.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Over a long session you have corrected Claude three times on the same pagination bug, and each new attempt reintroduces part of an earlier failed approach. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Run /clear and start over with a more specific prompt that captures what you have learned.
Correct Claude a fourth time, listing every previous failed approach that it should avoid.
Run /compact so the session keeps the history of attempts but in a summarized form.
