Switch to a model with a larger context window so the full history of attempts fits.

questions.explanation: After repeated corrections on the same issue, the context is cluttered with failed approaches that keep pulling Claude back. A clean session with a better prompt usually beats a long session with accumulated corrections. Another correction adds to the same clutter. Compacting or enlarging the context keeps the failed approaches in play, just summarized or with more room.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your CI review job runs Claude Code with -p and asks it to "list issues as JSON with file, line and severity." The script that posts inline PR comments fails a few times a week because the output includes prose or uses different key names. What change is most reliable?

options.text: Add few-shot examples of the desired JSON to the prompt and keep parsing stdout with a regex.
Pass the raw output to a second Claude call that converts whatever was returned into valid JSON for posting.
Switch to --output-format stream-json and assemble the findings from the streamed text events.
Use --output-format json with a --json-schema for the findings and read the structured_output field.

questions.explanation: --output-format json combined with --json-schema returns output that conforms to your schema in the structured_output field, which a posting script can rely on. The script should still check that the field is present, since a run can end without valid structured output. Few-shot examples improve format compliance probabilistically, but regex parsing of free text stays brittle. A conversion call adds cost and its own failure mode, and stream-json changes delivery, not structure.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your PR review job reruns on every push. Developers complain that each run reposts comments for issues that were already raised, including issues they have since fixed. What change best addresses this?

options.text: Lower the job's sensitivity so that later runs report only issues of critical severity.
Give Claude the prior run's findings and ask it to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
Run the review only on the first push of each PR and skip it for every later commit.
Have the posting script delete all earlier review comments on the PR before it posts the new set.

questions.explanation: Each run has no memory of earlier ones, so supplying the prior findings lets Claude separate new and still-open issues from ones already raised or fixed. That removes duplicates without losing coverage of new commits. Limiting later runs to critical issues hides legitimate findings. Reviewing only the first push misses bugs introduced later, and deleting and reposting comments destroys discussion threads while still repeating findings.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A CI job asks Claude Code to generate unit tests for changed modules. Reviewers find that many generated tests duplicate scenarios the existing suite already covers. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Tell Claude to generate fewer tests per module so that duplicates are less likely to appear.
Add a second pass that deletes any generated test whose name matches the name of an existing test.
Provide the module's existing test files in context so Claude targets scenarios not yet covered.
Raise the job's turn limit so Claude has more time to reason about gaps in test coverage.

questions.explanation: Claude can only avoid duplicating tests it can see, so including the existing test files lets it target uncovered behavior. Generating fewer tests reduces output without making it any less redundant. Name matching misses duplicates that have different names and can delete tests that share a name but differ in substance. More turns do not help when the existing suite is not in context.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Generated tests from your CI job pass but are low value: they assert trivial getters and build ad hoc mocks, even though the repository has shared fixtures for databases and queues. You want both CI runs and developers' local sessions to produce better tests. What should you do?

options.text: Document the testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and the available fixtures in the project CLAUDE.md.
Add a post-generation script that deletes any test shorter than ten lines before the PR is updated.
Put the standards only in the CI job's prompt string, since that is where most tests are generated.
Add the fixture documentation to each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so local runs improve first.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving project context such as testing standards, value criteria and fixture conventions to both CI-invoked and interactive Claude Code. One committed source improves every run that loads it. Deleting short tests filters on length, which does not measure value. A CI-only prompt leaves local sessions without the guidance, and user-level files are not shared with CI or teammates.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline has a Claude Code session generate a feature and then, in the same session, review its own diff before opening a PR. The self-review rarely flags anything, yet human reviewers keep finding real bugs. What is the best change?

options.text: Add "review critically and assume there are bugs" to the self-review prompt in the same session.
Run the review in a separate Claude Code invocation that has not seen the generation work.
Have the generating session review its diff twice and report only issues found both times.
Ask the generating session to rate its confidence in each change and flag any below a threshold.

questions.explanation: A session that wrote the code carries its own reasoning and assumptions into the review, which makes it less likely to question them. A fresh, independent instance reviews the diff without that bias. Adversarial wording in the same session does not remove the shared context. Requiring agreement across two self-reviews suppresses findings, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated in exactly the cases that matter.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. To speed up CI, someone added --bare to your review job's claude -p command. Since then, reviews ignore the review criteria and fixture conventions documented in the project CLAUDE.md. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: CLAUDE.md is never loaded in -p mode, so copy the criteria into every CI job's prompt string.
The CI runner is caching an old CLAUDE.md, so clear the runner cache before each review job.
The criteria are worded too softly, so rewrite them with MUST and NEVER so the review applies them.
--bare skips CLAUDE.md discovery, so remove it for this job or pass the criteria in explicitly.

questions.explanation: --bare starts Claude Code without auto-discovering CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills and similar configuration, so the project context stopped reaching the review. Either drop --bare for jobs that need project context or supply the criteria explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file. Without --bare, -p runs do load CLAUDE.md, so the first option misstates the behavior. A stale cache and soft wording do not explain a regression that began when the flag was added.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A nightly CI job runs claude -p to run the unit tests and fix failing ones. Logs show that Claude's attempts to run npm test are denied, so it gives up without fixing anything. You want the job to run unattended while granting no more than it needs. Which TWO changes are appropriate? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Pass --allowedTools with narrow rules such as "Bash(npm test *)", "Read" and "Edit".
Run the job with --dangerously-skip-permissions so that no tool call can ever be denied.
Add an allow rule for Bash(npm test *) to the permissions in the project's .claude/settings.json.
Remove -p from the command so that a maintainer can approve tool calls from the CI log.
Start the job with --permission-mode plan so that Claude can run its commands without any prompting.

questions.explanation: In non-interactive runs, a tool call that needs approval is denied unless something approves it, so the fix is to pre-approve exactly the tools the job needs. Narrow --allowedTools rules on the command line or an equivalent allow rule in the project's settings both do this. Skipping permissions grants far more than the job needs. Removing -p makes the job wait for interactive input that never comes, and plan mode blocks the edits the job exists to make.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your PR review prompt includes the instruction "check that code comments are accurate." Developers report that most comment-related findings are about slightly outdated wording, missing periods, or comments that could be clearer, while the comments they actually care about, ones that describe behavior the code no longer has, get buried. What is the most effective change to the prompt?

options.text: Add "only report comment issues you are highly confident about" so that borderline wording complaints are filtered out by the model.
Replace the instruction with a specific criterion: flag a comment only when the behavior it claims contradicts what the code actually does, and skip wording, grammar, and clarity suggestions.

Move comment checking into its own category and attach a numeric confidence score to each finding, so the pipeline can suppress low-scoring comment results before anything is posted to the pull request.
Ask the model to rank all comment findings by importance and post only the top three per pull request to limit noise.

questions.explanation: The root cause is a vague instruction that does not define what counts as an inaccurate comment, so the model reports everything that could loosely qualify. A categorical criterion (claimed behavior contradicts actual behavior) plus an explicit skip list tells the model exactly what to report. Confidence wording (A) and confidence scores (C) do not change what the model considers an issue, so the same wording complaints still pass. A top-three cap (D) is arbitrary and can drop real contradictions on large PRs while keeping trivia on small ones.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. After a week of complaints about noisy reviews, a teammate added "Be conservative. Only report high-confidence findings." to the review prompt. The false positive rate barely moved, and a few real bugs started going unreported. What should you do next?

options.text: Strengthen the wording with capital letters and repeat the instruction at the end of the prompt so the model weighs it more heavily.

Ask the model to output a 1-10 confidence score for every finding, and have the pipeline discard anything scored below 7 so that only the findings the model itself rates as strong are ever posted to developers.
Replace the general instruction with explicit categories to report (logic bugs, security issues, data loss risks) and categories to skip (style, naming, patterns consistent with local conventions).
Run the review twice on every pull request and post only the findings that appear in both runs.

questions.explanation: General instructions like "be conservative" fail because they do not tell the model which kinds of issues are in or out of scope; it simply becomes less willing to report anything, including real bugs. Specific categorical criteria for what to report and what to skip address the precision problem directly. Emphatic repetition (A) is still the same vague instruction. Self-reported confidence thresholds (B) and two-run intersection (D) filter by probability rather than defining the target, and intersection also suppresses real bugs that are caught intermittently.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your automated reviewer reports findings in four categories: security, correctness, performance, and maintainability. Dismissal data shows security and correctness findings are accepted about 85% of the time, but roughly 70% of performance findings are dismissed. Developers have started ignoring the bot entirely, including its security comments. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Temporarily disable the performance category so the high-precision categories regain developer trust, and rework the performance criteria before re-enabling it.
Keep all categories but prefix performance findings with a "low priority" label so developers know which comments they can safely skip.
Pause the entire reviewer until every category reaches the same acceptance rate, then relaunch it with an announcement to the team.
Add a footer to every review comment explaining that the bot can make mistakes and asking developers to read each finding carefully.

questions.explanation: High false positive categories erode trust in the accurate ones, which is exactly what the dismissal data shows. Turning off the noisy category restores the value of security and correctness findings right away while you improve the performance criteria. Labeling (B) still posts the noise that is training developers to ignore the bot. Pausing everything (C) throws away the categories that already work. A disclaimer (D) asks developers to absorb the cost of false positives instead of fixing their source.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. The same kind of defect, an unchecked null dereference in a request handler, was labeled "critical" on one pull request, "minor" on another, and "major" on a third. Teams use the severity label to decide whether to block a merge. How should you make severity classification consistent?

options.text: Reduce the scale to two levels, blocking and non-blocking, so the model has fewer boundaries to get wrong.
Require the model to write a one-paragraph justification of each severity it assigns before the label is posted to the pull request.
Lower the sampling temperature for review runs so the model produces the same label for the same input.
Define each severity level with explicit criteria and include a concrete code example for each level showing what qualifies.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent labels mean the model has no shared definition of each level, so it improvises. Explicit criteria per level, anchored by concrete code examples, give it a stable reference for classification. Collapsing to two levels (A) keeps the same undefined boundary and loses information teams use. A justification (B) explains an arbitrary choice without constraining it. Temperature (C) may reduce run-to-run variation on identical input but does nothing for similar defects in different code, which is the actual inconsistency.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. You are rewriting the system prompt for a pre-merge review job whose findings are mostly noise. Which TWO additions will most directly improve precision? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A defined list of issue types to report, such as logic errors, injection risks, and unhandled error paths, each with a one-line definition.
The sentence "Think very carefully and only report something if you are sure it is a problem."
A higher max_tokens value, so the model has enough room to consider every possible issue in the diff and explain each one fully before it answers.
An explicit list of things not to report, such as formatting, naming preferences, and code that follows the repository's existing conventions.
An instruction to report every potential issue so that developers, not the model, make the final call on each one.

questions.explanation: Precision improves when the prompt states which categories to report and which to skip, so the model knows where the boundary is. Options A and D define that boundary from both sides. Option B is the kind of general caution instruction that does not change what the model treats as an issue. A larger max_tokens (C) only allows longer output and does not affect which findings are reported. Reporting everything (E) maximizes false positives and pushes triage onto developers.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Developers complain that the review job keeps flagging long-standing problems in lines the pull request did not touch, which clutters the review and makes authors responsible for code they did not change. The model needs surrounding code to judge the diff correctly. What is the best fix?

options.text: Send only the changed lines to the model so it physically cannot comment on surrounding code that was not modified.
State an explicit scope rule: report issues introduced or modified by the diff, and mention pre-existing issues only when the change makes them newly reachable.
Instruct the model to focus on whatever matters most in the change and trust it to decide what is relevant to the author.
Ask the model to attach a confidence score to each finding, and have the pipeline suppress findings on unchanged lines whenever their score falls below a fixed threshold.

questions.explanation: The problem is that the prompt never defines review scope, so the model treats any visible defect as reportable. An explicit scope criterion keeps the surrounding context available for reasoning while limiting what gets reported, with a clear exception for issues the diff exposes. Stripping context (A) removes the information needed to catch bugs in the diff itself. "Focus on what matters" (C) is still vague. Confidence scores (D) measure certainty, not scope, so a confident finding on untouched code would still be posted.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts termination clauses from commercial contracts. Reviewers find that the model returns renewal terms, warranty expiration dates, and any sentence containing "end" or "expire" as termination clauses, so precision is poor. What change should you make first?

options.text: Ask the model to be precise and include only clauses it is confident are real termination clauses rather than related provisions.
Add a post-processing step that drops any extracted clause shorter than 20 words, since real termination clauses tend to be longer.
Define what qualifies, a provision giving a party the right to end the agreement and its conditions, and list look-alikes to exclude, such as renewal terms and obligation expiry dates.
Run every extracted clause through a second model call that asks whether it is really a termination clause, and keep only the clauses that this second call confirms as termination clauses.

questions.explanation: Low precision here comes from an undefined category: the model has no criterion separating termination rights from nearby concepts. Defining the category and naming the specific look-alikes to exclude fixes the root cause in one prompt change. A request for precision and confidence (A) does not supply the missing definition. A length filter (B) is an arbitrary heuristic unrelated to meaning. A second confirmation call (D) adds cost and still lacks the definition, so it inherits the same confusion; it might be useful later, but not as the first step.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your review job already returns findings through --json-schema with fields for file, line, severity, and suggested_fix, so every finding has all four fields. However, the suggested_fix values vary wildly: some contain a concrete code change, while others say only "consider refactoring this." What is the most effective way to make suggestions consistently actionable?

options.text: Add a few examples to the prompt showing complete findings whose suggested_fix contains a specific, minimal code change for the flagged line.
Add a minLength constraint to suggested_fix in the schema so that short, vague suggestions can no longer be produced.
Add a second paragraph of instructions describing in more detail what an actionable suggestion should contain and why it matters.
Post-process the output and delete findings whose suggested_fix does not contain a code block, so only concrete suggestions are posted.

questions.explanation: The schema already guarantees the fields exist; the inconsistency is in the quality of content, which is where few-shot examples are most effective. Showing complete findings with concrete fixes demonstrates the expected standard better than more prose instructions (C), which have already proven inconsistent. A length constraint (B) controls size, not specificity, and a long vague sentence would still pass. Deleting findings without code blocks (D) discards possibly real issues instead of improving how they are written.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your security review keeps flagging calls to the team's db.safeQuery() helper as SQL injection risks, even though the helper always uses parameterized queries. The codebase has several other internal helpers that sanitize input in similar ways, and new ones are added regularly. What is the best way to reduce these false positives?

options.text: List db.safeQuery() and every other sanitizing helper that exists today in the prompt, as functions that must never be flagged as injection risks under any circumstances by the reviewer.
Filter out any posted finding whose text mentions one of the known helper names before comments are published to the pull request.
Instruct the model to skip all database-related code during security review, since the team's helpers already cover that risk area.
Add a few examples contrasting a safe call through a parameterizing helper with a genuine issue, string concatenation into raw SQL, and explain why each was or was not flagged.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that distinguish acceptable patterns from genuine issues, with the reasoning shown, let the model generalize to helpers it has not seen, which matters because new helpers keep appearing. An allowlist (A) or a name-based filter (B) only covers known names and would also suppress a real misuse of a helper, such as passing concatenated SQL into it. Skipping all database code (C) removes coverage for exactly the area where injection bugs live.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. You extract the list of cited works from academic papers. Papers with a bibliography section extract well, but papers that cite sources inline, for example "(Okafor, 2019)" with no reference list, often return an empty citations array. What should you do?

options.text: Mark the citations array as required with a minimum of one item so the model cannot return it empty.
Add few-shot examples showing correct citation extraction from both a paper with a bibliography and a paper that uses only inline citations.
Build a classifier that detects the citation style first and routes each paper to a separate, style-specific extraction prompt maintained for that style.
Add the sentence "Look very carefully for citations anywhere in the document" to the extraction instructions.

questions.explanation: Empty results for one document structure indicate the model has not seen what correct extraction looks like for that structure. Examples covering both structures teach it to recognize inline citations as well as bibliographies. Forcing a non-empty array (A) pushes the model to fabricate entries for papers that truly cite nothing. A classifier and separate prompts (C) adds infrastructure before the cheaper fix has been tried. A generic "look carefully" instruction (D) does not show the model what an inline citation is.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts materials and quantities from field technicians' handwritten-style repair notes that were transcribed to text. Notes contain phrases like "a couple of brackets," "about 3 ft of conduit," and "a handful of screws." The model frequently outputs exact numbers such as quantity 2 or 37 screws that do not appear anywhere in the note. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Make the numeric quantity field required so every material has a value that downstream inventory systems can use directly.
Add a lookup table in post-processing that converts phrases like "a handful" or "a couple" into a standard numeric count after the extraction step has run for each note.
Add few-shot examples showing informal quantities captured as the original phrase with an approximate flag, and a numeric value only when the note states one.
Raise the sampling temperature slightly so the model explores alternatives instead of settling on one specific number.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are effective at reducing hallucination in extraction when inputs are informal, because they show exactly how to represent vague quantities without inventing precision. Requiring a number (A) is what drives the fabrication. A lookup table (B) runs after the model has already invented a number, so there is nothing informal left to convert. Raising temperature (D) increases variability and does nothing to stop invented values.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A nightly job asks Claude to write unit tests for recently changed functions. The generated tests nearly always cover only the happy path; error branches such as a timeout retry path or an early return for invalid input are rarely tested, even though the instructions say to "cover all branches." What should you add to the prompt?

options.text: Two or three examples that show a function, the untested branch identified in it, and a test written specifically to exercise that branch.
A requirement that every function receive at least five tests, so that more of the code paths are exercised.
A stronger instruction stating that complete branch coverage is mandatory and that missing branches will cause the job to fail.
A list of every branch type in the language, such as if, else, switch, catch, and early return, for the model to check against.

questions.explanation: The instruction already asks for branch coverage and is not producing it; few-shot examples demonstrate the judgment involved, spotting an untested branch and targeting it, which is what detailed instructions alone failed to convey. A test count (B) tends to produce more happy-path variants rather than different branches. A stronger mandate (C) repeats the same instruction with more pressure. A list of syntax constructs (D) does not show how to identify which branches lack tests or what a good branch test looks like.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your review prompt contains 40 example findings collected over several months, covering every category. The bot is still inconsistent on one ambiguous case: catch blocks that log an error and continue, which are sometimes acceptable and sometimes hide failures. What is the best change?

options.text: Add another 40 examples drawn from recent pull requests so the model sees a larger and more current sample of findings.
Replace the bulk with a small set of targeted examples on the log-and-continue boundary, each explaining why it was flagged or not versus the plausible alternative.
Keep the existing examples but remove their explanations, leaving only the code and the final label so the prompt stays shorter.
Move all 40 examples into a separate document and reference that document by name in the prompt, so that the instructions themselves are shorter and easier for the team to maintain.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples work best when they target the ambiguous case and show the reasoning that separates the chosen action from the plausible alternative. A large untargeted set dilutes the signal for the boundary that matters. Adding more general examples (A) makes that worse. Stripping explanations (C) removes exactly the reasoning the model needs to generalize. Referencing an external document by name (D) does not put the examples in the model's context at all.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your invoice extraction prompt has grown to 30 vendor-specific rules, such as "for Vendor X the total is in the footer" and "for Vendor Y dates are in the header." Each new vendor layout causes failures until someone adds another rule. What approach will best handle new layouts?

options.text: Continue adding a rule for each new vendor as soon as its first failure is reported, keeping the rule list current.
Detect the vendor from the document and route it to a dedicated prompt written for that vendor's specific layout, adding a new prompt whenever a vendor appears.
Fine-tune a custom model on several thousand labeled invoices so that it learns every vendor layout directly.
Replace most of the vendor rules with a few diverse examples that demonstrate how to locate totals and dates regardless of layout.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples let the model generalize the underlying judgment, where totals and dates tend to appear and how to recognize them, to layouts it has not seen, rather than matching only pre-specified cases. Adding rules (A) or per-vendor prompts (B) guarantees a failure for every new vendor before a fix exists. Fine-tuning (C) is far heavier than the problem warrants and is outside what this system needs to solve layout variation.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your pipeline asks Claude to "respond only with valid JSON" and parses the text response. About 2% of responses contain trailing commentary or a malformed bracket, which crashes the downstream loader. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Wrap the parser in a retry loop that resends the same request whenever JSON parsing fails, up to three times.
Add a regex-based repair step that strips any text outside the outermost braces and fixes common bracket and trailing-comma errors before the response is handed to the parser.
Define the extraction schema with schema enforcement, a strict tool or structured outputs, and read the validated result instead of parsing free text.
Repeat the JSON-only instruction at both the start and end of the prompt, in capitals, so the model gives it more weight.

questions.explanation: Schema-enforced output, either a tool with a JSON schema and strict mode or structured outputs, uses constrained decoding so the result is valid JSON matching the schema, which removes syntax errors at the source. Retries (A) and regex repair (B) treat symptoms and still fail on some responses. Repeating the instruction (D) keeps compliance probabilistic when the loader needs a guarantee.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system receives invoices, receipts, and purchase orders through the same inbox, and the type is not known in advance. You defined a separate extraction tool for each type. With tool_choice left at "auto," the model sometimes replies with a prose summary instead of calling any tool. Your model supports forced tool use. Which configuration fixes this?

options.text: Keep "auto" and add an instruction telling the model that it must always respond by calling one of the extraction tools.
Force the invoice extraction tool by name, since invoices are the most common document type arriving in the inbox.
Set tool_choice to "none" and include the three schemas in the system prompt so the model writes JSON that matches one of them.
Set tool_choice to "any" so the model must call one of the extraction tools but can still pick the one that matches the document.

questions.explanation: With "any," the model must call a tool but chooses which one, which is exactly right when several schemas exist and the document type is unknown. "Auto" plus an instruction (A) leaves a text-only reply possible. Forcing the invoice tool (B) would push receipts and purchase orders into the wrong schema. "None" (C) disables tools and returns to unenforced text JSON. Note that some newer models reject forced tool choice; on those, docs recommend "auto" with strict tools or structured outputs instead.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your workflow must run extract_metadata on every document before any enrichment tools (lookup_vendor, classify_spend) are called, because enrichment depends on the extracted vendor ID. Logs show the model sometimes calls lookup_vendor first using a guessed vendor name. Your model supports forced tool use. What should you do?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt stating that extract_metadata must always be the first tool called for every document.
On the first request, set tool_choice to force extract_metadata by name, then let later requests use automatic tool selection for enrichment.
Set tool_choice to "any" on the first request, so the model is required to call one of the available tools before it is allowed to produce any text.
Remove the enrichment tools from the request entirely and perform vendor lookup and spend classification by hand.

questions.explanation: Forcing a specific named tool guarantees that extraction runs first, which a downstream dependency requires; later turns can return to automatic selection. A prompt instruction (A) is probabilistic and is already being ignored in the logs. "Any" (C) forces some tool call but not which one, so lookup_vendor could still go first. Removing the enrichment tools (D) gives up the automation rather than ordering it.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your shipping-document schema marks purchase_order_number as required. Roughly a third of documents have no PO number at all, and auditors found that the model filled the field with plausible-looking but invented values. What is the best fix?

options.text: Make purchase_order_number optional and nullable, and instruct the model to return null when the document contains no PO number.
Add a validator that rejects responses with a missing PO number and retries the extraction with the validation error attached.
Add a regex pattern to the field so that only values matching the company's PO number format are accepted by the schema.
Add few-shot examples of real PO numbers so the model learns the expected format and stops producing unusual values.

questions.explanation: A required field gives the model no legitimate way to say the information is absent, so it fabricates a value to satisfy the schema. Making the field nullable, with an instruction to use null when absent, removes that pressure. Retrying (B) cannot succeed when the data is not in the document. A format pattern (C) and format examples (D) make fabricated values look more convincing without making them true.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your expense schema uses an enum category field with values hardware, software, and services. New spend types such as training courses and event sponsorships are being forced into the closest bucket, and genuinely ambiguous line items are assigned with false certainty. Which TWO schema changes best address this? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Add an "other" enum value paired with a category_detail string that captures what the item actually is.
Replace the enum with a free-text category string so the model can describe each item in its own words.
Add an "unclear" enum value for line items whose category cannot be determined from the document.
Expand the enum to 40 values covering every spend type the finance team can think of today.
Keep the enum unchanged but lengthen its description to explain the three categories in more detail.

questions.explanation: An "other" value with a detail string keeps the category extensible without losing structure, and an "unclear" value gives ambiguous items an honest home instead of a forced guess. Free text (B) throws away the consistency the enum provides for downstream systems. A 40-value enum (D) is speculative, still fails on the next new type, and makes selection harder. A longer description (E) cannot help when no listed value fits.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Source documents express dates as "03/04/24," "4 March 2024," and "2024-03-04," and some come from US offices while others come from European offices. Your strict schema defines invoice_date as a string, and the downstream system expects YYYY-MM-DD. Output dates are inconsistent and some day and month values are swapped. What should you do?

options.text: Leave the schema and prompt as they are and run a general-purpose date parsing library over the output to coerce every extracted value into YYYY-MM-DD.
Split date extraction into a separate model call per field so that each date receives the model's full attention.
Ask the model to copy each date exactly as written and let the downstream team decide how to interpret each format.
Add normalization rules to the prompt: output YYYY-MM-DD, resolve day-month order from the document's origin, and return null when ambiguous.

questions.explanation: A strict schema guarantees a string but not a consistent or correct format; normalization rules in the prompt alongside the schema tell the model how to convert values and how to resolve ambiguity using context only it can see. A parsing library (A) cannot tell whether 03/04/24 means March or April without the document's origin. Separate calls (B) add cost without addressing format. Copying raw text (C) pushes the same unresolved ambiguity downstream, minus the context needed to resolve it.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs claude -p to review a pull request, then a script posts each finding as an inline comment. The script currently parses Claude's prose with regular expressions and breaks whenever phrasing changes. What is the most robust approach?

options.text: Ask Claude in the prompt to put each finding on its own line using a fixed delimiter format and keep the regex-based parser.
Use --output-format json with a --json-schema defining the findings array, read the structured_output field, and check it is present first.
Use --output-format stream-json and reconstruct each finding from the text deltas as they arrive in the stream.
Keep plain text output, but send it to a second claude -p call that converts the prose review into JSON with the fields the comment-posting script expects.

questions.explanation: Claude Code's --json-schema with --output-format json returns output conforming to the schema in the structured_output field, which the script can consume directly; the docs advise checking that the field exists because a run can end without valid structured output. A delimiter convention (A) is still unenforced. Streaming deltas (C) is for real-time display and still yields free text. A second conversion call (D) adds cost and another unenforced step.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your validator flags invoices where the extracted line items do not sum to the extracted total. You want the retry request to give the model the best chance of correcting itself. Which TWO items should the retry include? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The original source document, so the model can re-read the line items and the total directly.
A shorter summary of the document instead of the full text, to keep the retry request inexpensive.
The failed extraction together with the specific validation error, for example that items sum to 1,240.00 but the total is 1,420.00.
A generic message saying only that the previous answer was wrong, with no further details, so that the model is not biased toward any one particular fix.
A higher temperature setting so the retry produces a meaningfully different answer from the first attempt.

questions.explanation: Effective retry-with-error-feedback includes the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error so the model can locate and fix the discrepancy. A summary (B) may drop the exact line items needed to find the error. A generic "wrong" message (D) gives the model nothing to act on. Raising temperature (E) just produces a different guess rather than a guided correction.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your retry loop resubmits extractions that fail validation. For one field, insurance_policy_number, retries almost never succeed. Investigation shows the contracts say "see attached Schedule B" for the policy number, and Schedule B is a separate file that the pipeline does not include. What should you change?

options.text: Increase the retry limit for this field from three attempts to five, since more attempts improve the odds of recovering the value.
Add an emphatic instruction that the policy number is always present somewhere in the contract and must be found.
Stop retrying this case: record the field as null with a reason that it is in an external document, and route it to fetch Schedule B or a human.
Switch retries for this field to the largest available model and give it a longer max_tokens budget so that it has the best chance of locating the value in the contract.

questions.explanation: Retries fix format and structural errors, but they cannot recover information that is absent from the input. Recognizing that the value lives in a document that was not provided, and recording it as missing with a reason for follow-up, is the correct handling. More retries (A) and a larger model (D) cannot find text that is not there. Insisting the value exists (B) pressures the model to fabricate one.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your team moved extraction to a strict tool schema and now proposes deleting the Pydantic validation layer because "the schema guarantees correct output." Which problem would still reach downstream systems if the validation layer were removed?

options.text: A response that is missing a key the schema lists as required, which would break the downstream loader.
A field returned as the string "12" when the schema specifies an integer, causing a type error downstream.
A response containing a malformed bracket or trailing comma that cannot be parsed as JSON at all.
The vendor's name extracted into the ship_to_address field while the schema's types and required fields are all satisfied.

questions.explanation: Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors, missing required fields, and type mismatches, but they do not check meaning; a value in the wrong field still satisfies the schema. Semantic validation, such as field-placement and cross-field checks, is still needed. Options A, B, and C are precisely the classes of error that schema enforcement prevents.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Finance reviewers want arithmetic discrepancies on invoices caught automatically. Some come from extraction mistakes and some from invoices that genuinely contain math errors. Which schema design best supports systematic detection?

options.text: Extract only stated_total and trust it, since the invoice's own total is the authoritative figure for payment.
Extract stated_total and calculated_total, the sum of extracted line items, and have code flag records where they differ.
Add an instruction asking the model to double-check that its arithmetic is correct before it returns the extracted invoice.
Extract the line items only and let downstream finance systems compute the total later when they process payments.

questions.explanation: Capturing both the stated total and a calculated total makes discrepancies visible and lets deterministic code flag them for review or retry, whichever side is wrong. Trusting stated_total (A) hides both extraction errors and genuine invoice errors. A double-check instruction (C) is probabilistic and leaves no signal for reviewers. Dropping the stated total (D) loses the comparison point needed to detect a mismatch.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Some vendor contracts contradict themselves: the cover page says payment terms are net 30 while the terms section says net 45. Your extraction silently picks one value, and accounts payable has paid on the wrong schedule several times. What is the best schema change?

options.text: Add a conflict_detected boolean and capture each conflicting value with its location, so conflicted records can be routed for review.
Instruct the model to always use the value from the detailed terms section, because detailed sections usually override cover pages in commercial contracts.
Instruct the model to use whichever value appears first in the document, so the choice is at least consistent.
Have the model compute and return the average of the conflicting values, so neither party is disadvantaged.

questions.explanation: When source data is internally inconsistent, the right behavior is to surface the conflict rather than resolve it invisibly; a conflict_detected flag plus both values and locations lets a human decide. A fixed precedence rule (B) or first-occurrence rule (C) is consistent but still silently wrong whenever the rule does not match the contract's intent. Averaging (D) invents a value that appears nowhere in the contract.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Developers dismiss about 40% of the review bot's findings, but the team cannot tell which kinds of code trigger the dismissed findings, so prompt improvements are guesswork. What should you add to make the feedback loop analyzable?

options.text: A required free-text field where developers must explain each dismissal in their own words before they are allowed to close the review comment.
A weekly report of the overall dismissal rate per repository, so the team can see whether the rate is improving.
A detected_pattern field on each structured finding naming the code construct that triggered it, logged alongside dismissal outcomes.
A cap of five findings per pull request so that developers have fewer comments to dismiss on each review.

questions.explanation: Tagging each finding with the construct that triggered it lets you group dismissals by pattern and identify exactly which criteria produce false positives. Free-text dismissal reasons (A) add developer friction and are hard to aggregate. An overall rate (B) shows that there is a problem but not where. A cap (D) hides findings without explaining which ones are wrong.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your validation layer flags several kinds of failures. Which TWO are likely to be fixed by retrying with the original document and the specific validation error? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The customer's name was placed in the account_manager field, while the correct name appears clearly in the document.
The contract value is defined only in an amendment that was not included in the documents sent to the model.
One line item was skipped, so the extracted items do not sum to the total that the document clearly states.
The signatory's name is fully redacted in the scanned source, so no name can be read anywhere in the file.
The source document itself contains a typo in its printed total, so its line items and its stated total never reconcile with each other.

questions.explanation: Retry with error feedback works when the correct information is in the document and the model made a placement or omission mistake, as in A and C. When the information lives in a document that was not provided (B) or is redacted (D), no retry can produce it. When the source itself is inconsistent (E), the right move is to flag the conflict rather than retry toward a reconciliation the document cannot support.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A partner contract requires that each document's extraction results be delivered within 36 hours of the document arriving. You will use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours, and your post-processing and delivery step takes about 2 hours. Documents arrive continuously. How often should you submit batches?

options.text: Every 24 hours, so that each batch contains a full day of documents and the per-request overhead is lowest.
Every 12 hours, which splits the day evenly and keeps batch counts low while staying comfortably close to the 36-hour target.
Every 8 hours, so a document's worst case is 8 hours waiting, 24 hours processing, and 2 hours delivery, within 36.
Never batch; send each document to the synchronous API as it arrives, since batch timing cannot be bounded.

questions.explanation: The worst case is the time a document waits for the next submission plus the 24-hour processing window plus delivery, so the submission interval must be at most 36 - 24 - 2 = 10 hours; every 8 hours meets that with margin. Every 24 hours (A) gives a worst case of 50 hours, and every 12 hours (B) gives 38 hours, both violating the contract. The synchronous API (D) meets the SLA but gives up the 50% batch discount when the processing window is bounded and can be planned around.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A batch of 10,000 document extractions finished. 9,860 succeeded, 120 errored because the documents exceeded the context window, and 20 expired. What is the most efficient recovery?

options.text: Resubmit the entire batch of 10,000 so that all results come from the same run and stay consistent with each other.
Resubmit all 140 failed requests unchanged in a new batch, since errored and expired requests are usually caused by transient load on the service.
Move the whole workload to the synchronous API, since the batch run has shown it cannot handle these documents.
Identify failures by custom_id, split the 120 oversized documents into chunks, and resubmit those plus the 20 expired requests.

questions.explanation: Each result is tied to its request by custom_id, so you can resubmit only the failures, with a fix where the failure has a known cause: oversized documents need chunking, while expired requests can be resent as they are. Resubmitting everything (A) pays again for 9,860 good results. Resending the oversized documents unchanged (B) will fail again for the same reason. Abandoning batch (C) gives up the savings over a fixable 1.4% failure rate.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your batch job stores results by position in the results file, assuming the first result matches the first request. Auditors found extracted data attached to the wrong source documents. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Give each request a custom_id derived from the source document's ID and join results to documents on that field.
Include the document ID in each prompt and instruct the model to repeat it at the start of its answer for matching.
Submit each document in its own one-request batch so that ordering can never be ambiguous between requests.
Sort the results file by completion timestamp before matching, so results line up with the order of submission.

questions.explanation: Batch results can come back in any order, so the docs direct you to match them using custom_id, which you set per request. Asking the model to echo an ID (B) makes correlation depend on model output when a deterministic field exists. One-request batches (C) defeat the purpose of batching. Completion timestamps (D) do not reflect submission order because requests are processed independently.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your nightly test-generation job is an agent that writes tests, runs them with a test-runner tool, reads failures, and revises them. To cut costs you want to move it to the Message Batches API. What should you understand before switching?

options.text: Batch requests cannot include tool definitions at all, so the test runner must be removed from the job and the tests written without any form of automated verification.
A batch request cannot run your tool mid-request and continue, so restructure into single-turn steps, run tests in your pipeline, and batch follow-ups.
Batch requests run the full agent loop automatically if tool_choice is set to "any," so only that setting needs to change.
Batch processing is only for document extraction workloads, so test generation must stay on the synchronous API.

questions.explanation: Each batch request is processed independently and asynchronously, so there is no way for your code to execute a client tool mid-request and send the result back within it; an iterative tool loop has to be restructured into separate single-turn requests. Batch requests can include tools (A is wrong), but tool_choice does not add an execution loop (C). Batch is suitable for any latency-tolerant workload, not just extraction (D), and nightly test generation is a good fit once restructured.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. You need to extract fields from 400,000 archived insurance documents with a new prompt that has only been tried on a handful of files. The job is latency tolerant. What is the best plan?

options.text: Submit all 400,000 documents immediately in the largest batches allowed and fix whatever fails during resubmission.
Split the archive into 40 equal batches and submit them all at once to finish the archive as quickly as possible.
Run the full archive through the synchronous API first to confirm quality, then switch to batches for any reruns.
Refine the prompt on a representative sample covering the document variants, check accuracy, then batch the full archive.

questions.explanation: Refining the prompt on a representative sample before large-scale batch processing maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying to reprocess thousands of documents after a prompt fix. Submitting everything first (A) or in parallel batches (B) multiplies the cost of any prompt defect across the whole archive. Running the full archive synchronously (C) pays full price for the very run that batch pricing was meant to discount.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your platform team runs five Claude workloads and wants to move the eligible ones to the Message Batches API for its cost savings. Which TWO are good candidates? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A weekly audit that scans every repository for deprecated API usage and emails a report on Monday morning.
A required status check that must pass before any pull request can be merged into the protected main branch of a repository.
A bot that replies when a developer mentions it in a pull request comment and asks a question.
A nightly job that drafts missing docstrings for functions merged that day, reviewed by engineers the next morning.
A release gate that summarizes changes and must finish before the deploy pipeline continues.

questions.explanation: Batch processing suits latency-tolerant, non-blocking work, because processing can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. The weekly audit (A) and nightly docstring drafts (D) are consumed hours later. The merge check (B) and release gate (E) block people or pipelines while they wait. The interactive reply bot (C) needs a prompt response to be useful.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline has Claude generate a fix for a failing test, then in the same session asks it to "review your change for bugs before we commit." The self-review almost never finds problems, yet human reviewers regularly catch logic errors in these fixes. What is the most effective improvement?

options.text: Enable extended thinking during the self-review step so the model reasons more deeply about its own change.
Strengthen the self-review prompt to say "be highly critical and assume there is at least one bug in your change."
Repeat the self-review three times in the same session and keep any issue raised in at least one of the runs.
Send the diff and the requirement to a separate Claude instance that has none of the generator's reasoning context.

questions.explanation: A model reviewing its own work in the same session retains the reasoning that produced the change and is less likely to question it. An independent instance without that context evaluates the diff on its merits and is more effective at catching subtle issues. Extended thinking (A) still reasons from inside the original context. A "be critical" instruction (B) can provoke invented issues without removing the anchoring. Repeated same-session reviews (C) share the same blind spot.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. You added an independent reviewer instance for generated code. To "give it full context," the pipeline passes it the generator's entire transcript, including its reasoning about why each decision was made. Since then the reviewer approves nearly everything. What should you change?

options.text: Tell the reviewer it must raise at least one issue per change so that it does not default to approval.
Pass the reviewer only the artifact and what it must satisfy, the diff, requirements, and tests, not the generator's reasoning.
Use the same model as the generator at a higher temperature so that its judgments diverge more often.
Pass the reviewer an even longer transcript that also includes the generator's earlier failed attempts, so it understands everything that was tried.

questions.explanation: An independent reviewer is valuable because it lacks the generator's reasoning; handing it that reasoning recreates the same anchoring that makes self-review weak. Give it the artifact and the criteria it must meet instead. A quota of issues (A) manufactures false positives. Temperature (C) adds randomness, not independence. More transcript (D) deepens the anchoring problem.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your review now runs a local pass on each changed file. On a recent pull request, one file changed get_user() to return null when a user is missing, and another file dereferences the result without a check. Neither per-file pass flagged it. What should you add?

options.text: A separate integration pass that receives a summary of each file's changed interfaces and their call sites, focused on cross-file data flow.
An instruction in each per-file pass to also consider how other files in the pull request might be affected by the change.
Deeper per-file passes with a longer prompt and more examples, so that each pass catches more subtle issues in its file.
A return to a single review pass over all of the changed files, since cross-file bugs can only be seen when every file is reviewed together in one context.

questions.explanation: Per-file passes are good at local issues but cannot see contracts that span files; a dedicated integration pass, fed with the changed interfaces and their callers, targets exactly that kind of bug. Asking per-file passes to consider other files (B) is impossible when those files are not in their context. Deeper per-file passes (C) still never see the caller. Returning to a single pass (D) brings back the attention dilution that caused the split in the first place.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. You want high-certainty review findings posted automatically and uncertain ones sent to a human triage queue, rather than treating all findings the same. How should you design this routing?

options.text: Instruct the review prompt to output only high-confidence findings, so that nothing uncertain is ever produced and the triage queue stays empty by design.
Post every finding automatically and ask developers to react with an emoji on the ones they consider uncertain.
Add a verification pass that reports confidence for each finding, calibrate thresholds against labeled past findings, and route on them.
Have the model score each finding from 1 to 10 and send anything below 8 to triage, using that threshold as-is.

questions.explanation: A verification pass that attaches confidence to each finding enables routing, and calibrating the thresholds against labeled historical outcomes is what makes the scores trustworthy, since raw self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated. Filtering at generation time (A) relies on the same vague caution instruction that fails to improve precision and gives you nothing to route. Posting everything (B) skips routing entirely. An uncalibrated fixed cutoff (D) assumes the model's scale means something it may not.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. You extract obligations from 150-page master service agreements in a single request. Obligations in the middle sections are frequently missed, and those that depend on defined terms from the definitions section are sometimes extracted incorrectly. What architecture best addresses both problems?

options.text: Ask for a higher max_tokens on the single request so the model has more room to list obligations from every section.
Extract per section in focused passes with the definitions section included, then run a consolidation pass to merge and resolve cross-references.
Run the single-request extraction three times and keep only obligations that appear in at least two of the runs.
Shorten each contract by summarizing every section first, then extract the obligations from the combined section summaries in one final consolidated request.

questions.explanation: Focused per-section passes avoid the attention dilution that causes mid-document misses, supplying the definitions keeps each pass accurate, and a consolidation pass handles cross-section references and duplicates. Raising max_tokens (A) only allows a longer answer and does not change how attention is spread over the input. Majority voting (C) suppresses obligations that are caught only intermittently, which are exactly the missed ones. Summarizing first (D) risks dropping the precise obligation language you need to extract.

questions.question: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your review system runs several reviewer agents in parallel, each looking for different issue types. Developers complain about duplicate comments on the same line, occasional contradictory advice, and findings that turn out to be wrong when checked against the code. What should you add before results are posted?

options.text: A rule that a finding is posted only when at least two of the parallel agents independently report the same issue.
A consolidation into one reviewer agent that handles all issue types, so that only a single set of findings is ever produced.
A voting feature that lets developers upvote or downvote each comment after it is posted, to train future reviews.
A verification stage that checks each candidate finding against the code, then deduplicates and ranks what remains.

questions.explanation: A verification step that checks findings against the code filters false positives, and deduplication and ranking resolve repeated or conflicting comments before anything reaches developers; this mirrors how Claude Code's managed Code Review is structured. Requiring agreement (A) suppresses real issues that only the agent specialized in that issue type would find. A single agent (B) gives up the coverage of specialized parallel reviewers. Post-hoc voting (C) still exposes developers to the noise.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Long sessions are condensed with a rolling summary once they pass a token threshold. QA finds that late in these sessions the agent tells customers their refund is 'around fifty dollars' when the order showed $57.38, and forgets that the customer was promised delivery by Friday. What change most reliably prevents this?

options.text: Run the rolling summarization more often so each summary covers fewer turns and drops less detail.
Keep amounts, dates, order numbers and promises in a case facts block sent with every prompt, outside the summary.
Add an instruction to the summarization prompt asking it to stay precise whenever it mentions any numbers, dates or promises.
Turn off summarization and rely on a larger context window to keep the entire raw transcript available.

questions.explanation: Progressive summarization tends to blur exact values and customer-stated expectations, so transactional facts belong in a persistent structured block that is never summarized. More frequent summarization (A) still passes facts through a lossy step repeatedly. A precision instruction (C) is probabilistic and does not remove the lossy compression. Dropping summarization (D) does not scale and long raw transcripts invite the lost-in-the-middle problem.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Each lookup_order call returns about 45 fields (warehouse codes, carrier internals, tax breakdowns), but return decisions only need status, purchase date, item, amount and return eligibility. Customers with several orders push the session close to the context limit and the agent starts missing details. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Tell the agent in the system prompt to ignore fields that are not relevant to the customer's current request.
Summarize the whole conversation every three turns so older order lookups take up less room in context.
Split lookup_order into many narrow tools that each return one field, so the agent requests only what it needs.
Trim each lookup_order result to the return-relevant fields before it is added to the conversation context.

questions.explanation: Tool results accumulate in context and consume tokens out of proportion to their relevance, so filtering them to the needed fields before they enter context fixes the root cause. Telling the model to ignore fields (A) still spends the tokens. Frequent summarization (B) adds a lossy step and can blur exact order facts. Dozens of single-field tools (C) is over-engineered and multiplies tool calls and selection errors.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The coordinator concatenates outputs from twelve subagents into one long input for the synthesis agent. Reports consistently reflect findings from the first and last few subagents but often omit important findings from those in the middle. How should you restructure the synthesis input?

options.text: Shuffle the order of subagent outputs on each run so that no single subagent is consistently placed in the middle.
Append a closing instruction telling the synthesis agent to give every subagent's findings equal consideration.
Open with a key findings summary, then put each subagent's detailed results under explicit section headers.
Raise max_tokens on the synthesis call so the agent has enough output budget to cover every subagent's findings.

questions.explanation: Models handle the beginning and end of long inputs most reliably, so leading with a key findings summary and giving detailed results clear section headers mitigates the position effect. Shuffling (A) just moves which findings get dropped. A closing instruction (B) does not change how attention falls across a long input. max_tokens (D) limits output length and does not affect how well the input is processed.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A team rebuilds the agent directly on the Messages API. To save tokens, each request sends only the system prompt and the newest user message. Customers now complain that the agent asks again for the order number they gave two turns earlier. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Send the complete conversation history, including prior tool calls and results, with every request to the API.
Enable prompt caching so the earlier turns are cached on the server side and recalled in later requests.
Increase max_tokens on each request so the model can keep more of the earlier conversation in memory.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to remember every identifier the customer has already given.

questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless, so conversational coherence requires sending the full history on each request. Prompt caching (B) speeds up reuse of a prefix you still send yourself and does not add memory. max_tokens (C) caps output length and has nothing to do with recall. A remember instruction (D) cannot help because the earlier turns are simply not in the request.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Document analysis subagents each return several thousand words of prose including their full reasoning. The synthesis agent has a tight context budget, so it truncates inputs and produces reports with undated claims and missing sources. Which TWO changes to the upstream subagents best address this? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Have the coordinator keep only the first 1,000 tokens of each subagent's output before passing it on.
Return structured key facts with citations and relevance scores instead of verbose prose and reasoning.
Have the synthesis agent summarize each subagent's output in a separate pass before it starts writing.
Remove citations from the subagent outputs so the remaining content fits inside the synthesis budget.
Include metadata such as dates, source locations and methodology with each finding.

questions.explanation: When the downstream agent has a limited budget, upstream agents should return compact structured data (B) and attach the metadata synthesis needs to attribute and date claims correctly (E). Truncating to the first 1,000 tokens (A) cuts arbitrarily and loses findings. An extra summarization pass (C) adds cost and another lossy step without fixing the format. Removing citations (D) destroys provenance the reports require.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer's first message is: 'I don't want a bot. Put me through to a person.' Their underlying issue, a shipping address change, is something the agent could complete in one tool call. How should the agent respond?

options.text: Make the address change first because it is quick, then offer the transfer if the customer still wants a person.
Verify identity and investigate the account fully first, so the human agent receives a complete case file.
Call escalate_to_human right away with a short summary of the request, without attempting to resolve it.
Check the sentiment of the message and transfer only if the customer's tone crosses a frustration threshold.

questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human should be honored immediately, without first attempting investigation or resolution. Resolving first (A) overrides the customer's stated preference even if the task is easy. Investigating first (B) delays the handoff the customer asked for. Sentiment gating (D) is an unreliable proxy and ignores an explicit request.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer writes angrily that their package is late for the third time. They have not asked for a human, and a late-delivery credit is clearly within policy and the agent's tools. What is the best behavior?

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration, offer the credit, and escalate only if the customer then says they want a person.
Escalate to a human at once, because repeated problems and strong negative emotion together signal a high-risk case.
Apply the credit without engaging with the complaint, since the emotional content does not affect the policy.
Ask the customer to rate their frustration from 1 to 10 and escalate whenever the rating is above seven.

questions.explanation: When the issue is within the agent's capability, the agent should acknowledge the frustration and offer resolution, escalating only if the customer reiterates a preference for a human. Escalating on emotion (B) treats sentiment as a proxy for complexity and hurts first-contact resolution. Ignoring the complaint (C) solves the issue but handles the customer poorly. A frustration rating (D) is another sentiment proxy and adds friction.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer asks the agent to match a lower price they found at a competitor. The refund policy covers price adjustments when your own site lowers its price but says nothing about competitor prices. Logs show the agent sometimes approves these and sometimes refuses. What should the agent be designed to do?

options.text: Approve the adjustment, since a competitor match is a close analogy to the own-site case the policy allows.
Refuse the adjustment, since the policy does not list competitor matching among the allowed adjustments.
Decide case by case and proceed only when the agent's self-reported confidence in its reading is high.
Escalate to a human, because the policy is silent on this request and it requires a policy decision.

questions.explanation: When policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific request, that gap is an escalation trigger, not something the agent should resolve by interpretation. Approving by analogy (A) and refusing by omission (B) both have the agent invent policy, which explains the current inconsistency. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated and does not resolve a genuine policy gap.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. A customer gives only their name, and get_customer returns three accounts with that name in the same state. The agent currently picks the account with the most recent activity, which occasionally leads to discussing another person's orders. What is the right fix?

options.text: Have the agent pick the account whose recent orders best match the products the customer has mentioned.
Have the agent ask for another identifier, such as email or an order number, when several accounts match.
Change get_customer to return only its single highest-ranked match so that the agent never sees multiple accounts at once.
Escalate every lookup that returns more than one account to a human so that none are misidentified.

questions.explanation: Multiple matches call for clarification with additional identifiers, not heuristic selection. Matching on mentioned products (A) is still a heuristic guess with privacy consequences when wrong. Returning only the top match (C) hides the ambiguity and makes the guess invisible. Escalating every multi-match (D) sends a problem the agent can resolve itself to humans and hurts first-contact resolution.

questions.question: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are writing explicit escalation criteria, with few-shot examples, for the system prompt. Which TWO conditions should be listed as escalation triggers? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The customer explicitly asks to speak with a human agent.
The customer's recent messages fall below a negative sentiment score threshold set in advance.
The request needs a policy exception or falls in a gap the policy does not address.
The agent rates its own confidence below 7 out of 10 for its planned reply.
The conversation has gone past a fixed number of turns or tool calls.

questions.explanation: Appropriate triggers include an explicit customer request for a human (A) and policy exceptions or gaps (C), along with an inability to make meaningful progress. Sentiment (B) and self-reported confidence (D) are unreliable proxies for actual case complexity. A fixed turn or tool-call count (E) measures length, not whether the agent can resolve the case.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The web search subagent returns an empty list both when its search backend times out and when a query genuinely finds nothing. The coordinator then writes 'no published research exists' for topics that were simply never searched. What change fixes this?

options.text: Have the subagent report an access failure as a distinct error status, separate from a successful empty search.
Have the coordinator automatically re-run every search that comes back empty before drawing any conclusion from it.
Have the subagent raise its timeouts as exceptions that stop the research workflow until an operator restarts it.
Add guidance to the coordinator prompt telling it to treat empty search results with a healthy degree of skepticism.

questions.explanation: The coordinator can only choose correctly if access failures (which may need a retry) are distinguishable from valid empty results (which are real findings). Re-running every empty result (B) wastes calls on genuine no-match queries and still cannot tell the cases apart. Halting the workflow (C) is an overreaction to a single failure. Prompting for skepticism (D) asks the model to guess at information the response does not contain.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document analysis subagent sends every error back to the coordinator, including brief 503 responses that succeed on a second try. The coordinator's context fills with error traffic and it frequently re-plans tasks that would have worked moments later. What is the best error-handling design?

options.text: Move all retry logic into the coordinator so a single component sees and manages every failure across the system.
Have the subagent swallow any error it encounters and continue, returning whatever results it managed to collect.
Have the subagent retry transient failures itself and escalate only unresolved errors, with attempts and partial results.
Shorten the coordinator's system prompt so more of its context window is left free for the error messages coming from subagents.

questions.explanation: Subagents should recover locally from transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve, including what was attempted and any partial results. Centralizing retries (A) is the current problem: it floods the coordinator with noise. Swallowing errors (B) hides real failures and produces incomplete research marked as complete. Freeing context (D) treats the symptom and leaves the noisy design in place.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Two of five source databases were unreachable during a run. The coordinator correctly continued with the remaining sources, but the final report reads as equally confident on every subtopic, and stakeholders did not realize some areas had almost no supporting evidence. What should change?

options.text: Stop report generation whenever any source is unavailable so that no report is ever produced from partial data.
Keep retrying the unreachable databases until every one responds before the synthesis step is allowed to begin.
Add a standard disclaimer to every report noting that some sources may not have been reachable at the time of research.
Have synthesis annotate coverage: which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps from missing sources.

questions.explanation: Coverage annotations tell readers exactly which findings are well supported and which topic areas are thin because sources were unavailable. Refusing to produce any report (A) discards useful partial work. Retrying until everything responds (B) can block indefinitely. A generic disclaimer (C) appears on every report and does not say which conclusions are weak.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. An extraction subagent processing a 200-page contract fails at page 181 because of a corrupted scan, after extracting valid data from pages 1-180. The orchestrator currently discards everything for that document and queues it to start over. What is the better approach?

options.text: Keep discarding and reprocessing the whole document, since a partial extraction cannot be trusted in any way.
