Return the extracted data with a structured error naming the failure and unprocessed pages, so only the gap is redone.
Mark the document as successfully processed using the fields extracted so far, leaving the missing ones empty.
Fail the entire batch so an operator can investigate the corrupted scan before any further documents in it are processed.

questions.explanation: Structured error context that includes partial results and exactly what failed lets the orchestrator keep valid work and route only the remaining pages for retry or review. Discarding everything (A) wastes valid work and will likely fail again at the same page. Marking it a success (C) silently suppresses the error and sends incomplete data downstream. Failing the batch (D) stops unrelated documents over one bad file.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The document analysis subagent receives a 403 'subscription required' response for a key journal article. It retries five times with exponential backoff, which adds several minutes, then reports a generic failure. What should it do instead?

options.text: Report a non-retryable access error at once, with the source tried and alternatives such as a preprint.
Increase the retry count and backoff ceiling, since publisher access errors often clear up when given enough time.
Return an empty result marked as successful so the coordinator continues as if the article contained nothing useful.
Stop the whole research task, because missing a key source means the final report can no longer be relied upon.

questions.explanation: A permission error is not transient, so retrying wastes time; the subagent should propagate it immediately with the failure type, what was attempted and possible alternatives so the coordinator can recover. More retries (B) repeats the mistake. Reporting false success (C) suppresses the error and hides a coverage gap. Terminating the workflow (D) ignores recovery options that could still succeed.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. After a two-hour session mapping a legacy billing system, Claude's answers become inconsistent, and it starts describing 'the typical repository pattern' instead of the specific InvoiceLedgerStore class it found an hour earlier. You still have many questions to ask about this code. What is the most effective practice?

options.text: Paste a long recap of everything discovered so far into each new question so the details stay close at hand.
Have Claude record key findings, such as class names and file paths, in a scratchpad file it rereads later.
Run /clear and restart the investigation from scratch, since a fresh context window will produce more consistent answers.
Keep the session going and correct Claude by hand each time it falls back on generic descriptions of the code.

questions.explanation: A scratchpad file persists specific findings outside the degrading conversation, and Claude can reread it to counteract context degradation in long sessions. Pasting a recap into every question (A) inflates context further and is error-prone. /clear (C) throws away two hours of discovery with nothing kept. Manual correction (D) treats symptoms while degradation continues.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Before refactoring the refund module, you need answers to 'which test files exercise refund logic?' and 'what does the refund flow depend on?'. Earlier attempts to search directly filled the main session with hundreds of grep and file-read results, leaving little room for the refactor. How should you get these answers?

options.text: Run the searches in the main session as before, then ask Claude to forget the raw output once it has answered.
Use @imports in CLAUDE.md to load all refund-related source files at startup so no searching is needed.
Ask Claude to read every file in the refund directory up front so the answers come from complete information.
Have Claude delegate each question to a subagent that explores separately and returns only a concise summary.

questions.explanation: Subagents run in their own context window, so verbose exploration output stays there and only the summary returns, keeping the main session free for coordination and the refactor. Asking Claude to forget output (A) does not remove anything from context. Importing source files through CLAUDE.md (B) loads them into every session's context. Reading every file up front (C) is the same flooding problem on a larger scale.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Phase one subagents established which regulations apply and which sources are unreliable. In phase two, newly spawned subagents keep citing the unreliable sources and re-researching settled questions. The coordinator's delegation prompts just say 'continue building on our earlier findings'. What should the coordinator do?

options.text: Nothing more is needed in the prompt, since spawned subagents inherit the coordinator's history once they start.
Pass the complete transcripts of every phase-one subagent into each new phase-two subagent's starting context window.
Summarize the key phase-one findings, including excluded sources, and inject that summary into each phase-two prompt.
Give the phase-two subagents a tool that lets them search through the coordinator's own conversation history.

questions.explanation: A newly spawned subagent starts with a fresh context and sees only what the coordinator passes in its prompt, so key findings must be summarized and injected explicitly. Assuming inheritance (A) is the misconception causing the bug. Full transcripts (B) waste each subagent's budget on verbose detail. A history search tool (D) is over-engineered and leaves it to chance whether the subagent finds the decisions.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A research job that runs for several hours occasionally crashes partway through. After a restart, the coordinator has no record of which subtasks finished or what they found, so it repeats all completed work. What design best supports recovery?

options.text: Raise the job's timeout limits and rerun the job, so that crashes caused by long execution become less frequent.
Have each agent export structured state to a known location, and load that manifest on resume into prompts.
Keep full transcripts of all agents in log storage so an engineer can review what happened after each crash.
Collapse the system into one agent so there is no coordination state that could be lost when a crash occurs.

questions.explanation: Structured state exports in a known location give the coordinator a manifest it can load on resume, letting it skip finished subtasks and inject their results into agent prompts. Longer timeouts (A) do not address crashes from other causes and still lose progress. Transcript logs (C) help debugging but are not a machine-usable recovery mechanism. One agent (D) gives up the benefits of parallel specialization and still loses progress on a crash.

questions.question: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. During a long exploration session, the context has filled with verbose discovery output. You want to keep working on the same task without losing the list of files you have modified and the test commands you settled on. Which TWO actions best accomplish this? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Run /clear to reset the context, then describe the task again from memory alone.
Turn off automatic compaction so nothing from the session gets summarized.
Run /compact with instructions to keep the modified files and test commands.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction saying what compaction must always preserve.
Start a separate terminal session and paste the last few messages into it.

questions.explanation: /compact with focus instructions (C) shrinks the context while telling the summary what to keep, and a CLAUDE.md compaction instruction (D) applies that guidance every time compaction runs. /clear (A) discards everything and relies on memory. Disabling auto-compaction (B) lets the context keep filling with low-value output. A new session with a few pasted messages (E) loses most of what was learned.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your pipeline extracts fields from invoices, purchase orders and customs forms, and it shows 97% field accuracy on last month's audited sample. Operations wants to remove human review for all extractions next week. What should you do before agreeing?

options.text: Approve the change, since 97% accuracy is above the 95% bar the business set when the pipeline launched.
Require overall accuracy to reach 99% on the next monthly sample, then remove review for all extractions.
Break accuracy down by document type and by field to confirm that every segment performs well enough.
Keep a uniform 1% random sample under human review after removal, so overall accuracy can still be tracked.

questions.explanation: An aggregate figure can hide poor performance on a specific document type or field, so accuracy should be validated by segment before reducing human review. Approving on the aggregate (A) or a higher aggregate (B) leaves the same blind spot. A uniform 1% sample (D) is useful for monitoring but too thin to reveal weak segments before the decision is made.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. High-confidence extractions are now written straight to the ERP system, and only low-confidence ones go to reviewers. Leadership asks how you will know if error rates among the auto-approved extractions rise, or if a new type of error appears. What is the best approach?

options.text: Have reviewers check a stratified random sample of high-confidence extractions across document types and fields.
Keep reviewing only low-confidence extractions, since high-confidence ones have already proven reliable.
Rely on downstream teams to report problems they notice in the ERP and investigate each report they file.
Review the first hundred high-confidence extractions processed each morning as a daily quality check.

questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence output measures ongoing error rates in every segment and surfaces novel error patterns. Reviewing only low-confidence items (B) never observes errors in the auto-approved stream. Downstream complaints (C) are late and incomplete. The first hundred each morning (D) is a convenience sample that may systematically miss certain document types.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. The model outputs a confidence score for each field, and anything at 0.9 or above skips review. That threshold was chosen by intuition. Audits show date fields scored at 0.9 or above are wrong 12% of the time, while totals at the same score are almost always right. How should you set review thresholds?

options.text: Change the prompt to ask the model to assign lower confidence scores whenever it extracts a date field.
Average the field scores into a single document score and route whole documents using that average.
Raise the threshold for every field to 0.99 so that only the most certain extractions skip human review.
Calibrate a separate threshold for each field against a labeled validation set of known correct values.

questions.explanation: Raw confidence scores are only useful for routing once they are calibrated against labeled data, and the audit shows calibration differs by field. Prompting for lower date scores (A) shifts numbers without grounding them in measured accuracy. A document average (B) hides exactly the field-level differences the audit found. A blanket 0.99 (C) over-routes reliable fields and is still uncalibrated for dates.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. The review team can check about 300 of the 2,000 documents processed each day. Which TWO criteria should decide which documents are routed to them? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: One or more fields fall below their calibrated confidence threshold.
The document comes from one of the company's largest customers.
The document is among the longest received in that day's intake.
The source itself is ambiguous or contradictory, such as two totals.
The document arrived during the first part of the processing day.

questions.explanation: Limited reviewer capacity should go to extractions where the model is least reliable (A) and where the source document is ambiguous or contradictory (D), since those are most likely to be wrong. Customer size (B) and document length (C) are not direct signals of extraction error. Arrival time (E) is arbitrary and spends capacity without regard to risk.

questions.question: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. You are about to calibrate field-level confidence thresholds. The only labeled validation set available contains 500 typed vendor invoices, but production also includes scanned handwritten receipts and multi-page customs declarations. What should you do before relying on the calibrated thresholds?

options.text: Calibrate on the typed invoices and apply those thresholds to all document types, since the fields are similar.
Skip calibration and use the model's raw confidence scores, since the labeled data is not fully representative.
Build labeled samples for each production document type and calibrate and validate thresholds per segment.
Increase the typed invoice set to 5,000 examples so the calibration has greater statistical confidence overall.

questions.explanation: Calibration is only valid for the kinds of documents it was measured on, so each production segment needs labeled data before its thresholds can be trusted. Transferring typed-invoice thresholds (A) assumes the model behaves the same on very different inputs. Raw scores (B) are uncalibrated and unsafe for routing. A larger typed-only set (D) tightens the estimate for the wrong population.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Fact-checkers find that many report citations point to sources that do not contain the cited claim. Tracing the pipeline shows that document analysis subagents return prose summaries, and the report agent later attaches citations by matching claims to the list of sources consulted. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a final pass in which the report agent searches the web again to locate a source for each claim it makes.
Have subagents output claim-source mappings (URL, document, excerpt) kept and merged through synthesis.
Replace inline citations with a bibliography of every consulted source, listed together at the end of the report.
Instruct the report agent to take extra care to match each of its claims to the most relevant source it can find.

questions.explanation: Attribution is lost when findings are compressed without their sources, so subagents must emit structured claim-source mappings that every later stage preserves. Re-searching afterward (A) is post-hoc and can attach a source that does not actually support the claim. A bibliography (C) gives up claim-level attribution. A care instruction (D) leaves the lossy pipeline unchanged.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. While analyzing a company, the document analysis subagent finds that the annual filing reports 12% revenue growth while the investor presentation states 14%. Today it stops and returns only an error saying the sources conflict. How should it handle this?

options.text: Report the figure from the annual filing alone, because regulatory filings are generally the more authoritative source.
Report 13% as a reasonable midpoint between the two figures, so the synthesis step gets a single clean value to use.
Keep stopping on conflicts, but add an error code that tells the coordinator which specific field could not be resolved.
Finish the analysis with both figures annotated by source, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile.

questions.explanation: Conflicting values from credible sources should be kept and annotated with attribution, and the analysis completed so the coordinator can reconcile them before synthesis. Picking one source (A) discards information, possibly a legitimate definitional difference. Averaging (B) invents a number neither source reports. Halting with a better error code (C) still blocks the rest of the analysis over a normal situation.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A report on remote-work adoption flags a 'major contradiction' between one survey reporting 31% and another reporting 52%. In fact, the surveys were conducted five years apart and reflect a trend. The subagents' outputs contained the figures and sources but no dates. What change best prevents this?

options.text: Require subagents to include publication and data collection dates with each finding they output.
Instruct the synthesis agent to drop any source more than three years old so the comparisons stay current.
Send every pair of differing statistics to a human reviewer before the synthesis agent is allowed to proceed.
Tell the synthesis agent to assume that any two differing figures most likely come from different time periods.

questions.explanation: Without dates, synthesis cannot tell temporal change from genuine disagreement, so subagents must report publication or collection dates in their structured output. Dropping older sources (B) discards the very data that shows the trend. Sending every difference to humans (C) is expensive and still leaves reviewers without the dates. Assuming a time difference (D) replaces one guess with another and would hide real contradictions.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Reviewers say reports on a drug's effectiveness read as uniformly authoritative. Findings replicated across large trials sit next to claims from one small observational study, with no way to tell them apart. The source data is accurate. How should the report structure change?

options.text: Have the synthesis agent add its own confidence score, from 1 to 10, after every sentence in the final report.
Remove any finding that is supported by only one study, so that the report includes only replicated results.
Separate well-established and contested findings into explicit sections, keeping methodology context.
Move the details about each study's size and design into footnotes so the main body of the text reads cleanly.

questions.explanation: Explicit sections for well-established versus contested findings, with the original source characterizations and methodology kept, let readers weigh evidence correctly. Per-sentence self-reported scores (A) are uncalibrated and clutter the report. Dropping single-study findings (B) removes potentially important emerging evidence. Footnotes (D) bury the context readers need to see whether a claim is contested.

questions.question: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. Market reports combine quarterly financial figures for eight competitors, recent news coverage, and technical comparisons of their products. The report agent currently renders all of it as bullet lists, and readers struggle to compare financials or follow the news context. What should the report agent do?

options.text: Keep bullet lists for every section, because one consistent format makes reports easier to scan quickly.
Render each content type suitably: financials as tables, news as prose, technical findings as lists.
Output the entire report as structured JSON so readers can load it into whatever format tools they prefer.
Produce three separate reports, one for each content type, so that each can use its own single format.

questions.explanation: Synthesis output should match format to content: tables make financial figures comparable, prose carries news context, and structured lists suit technical findings. A uniform bullet format (A) is the cause of the current problem. JSON (C) moves the presentation work onto readers. Separate reports (D) break the integrated analysis readers need when linking financials, news and products.
